subtopic: NATO-STATEMENT FOLLOWING PARIS MEETING OF DEFENCE MINISTERS

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Hellyer (Minister of National Defence):
subtopic: NATO-STATEMENT FOLLOWING PARIS MEETING OF DEFENCE MINISTERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to give a brief report of the meeting of NATO Defence Ministers held in Paris on Monday and Tuesday. You may recall that a decision was taken at the Council of Ministers held in Ottawa in May, 1963 to commence a study of strategy, force goals and the use of economic resources. A study has been undertaken by the Council in permanent session, constituted as a military committee and working in cooperation with the major NATO military commanders.
In considering the question of strategy a theoretical discussion arose which indicated a rather sharp divergence of views. A preliminary report was presented to the Council of Ministers in December last, for their consideration.
In the December discussion it seemed apparent to me that the divergence of opinion related more to the theoretical discussion than to the real contingencies with which the Alliance might be faced. With this thought in mind, I suggested holding a Defence Ministers Meeting with the object of examining the real situation in the hope that the wide areas of agreement would come into focus and the differences, if they exist, would prove to be largely irrelevant. The suggestion, which was supported by one or two other Ministers, included the recommendation that the meeting be as informal as possible to permit a full, frank exchange of views on vital issues.
The conference which concluded Tuesday afternoon was even more productive than I had hoped for. A consensus did emerge to the effect that the differences were largely theoretical and that the areas of agreement are in fact very great. Agreement was reached and decisions taken which provide the political direction for the Military Committee in the continuation of its studies in the months ahead. I think it is fair to say that the informality of the restricted session assisted
Ministers in reaching a consensus and taking the necessary action.
One of the most important decisions was in respect of force goals for the next planning period. It was the opinion of Ministers that force goals should not be unrealistic in calling for increases in manpower and expenditure obviously and demonstrably well beyond any possibility of implementation. The Ministers, therefore, directed the Military Committee to continue the study of realistic force goals, in co-operation with the military commanders, to the end that they be ready for consideration by the Council of Ministers in December.
[DOT] (2:40 p.m.)
The Military Committee was instructed to undertake studies on a number of other subjects, including certain specific contingencies. One area of particular interest to Canada is consideration of NATO's capability to respond to aggression on the northern or southeastern flanks. Last year Canada committed a battalion group to the Allied Command Europe Mobile Force for possible employment with the balance of the force on the flanks. As Canada has adopted a policy of developing a mobile force with a global capability, I indicated our willingness to consider to what extent our forces might co-operate with similar forces from other members of the alliance.
As has been reported in the press, the United States has proposed a committee of four or five Ministers of Defence to consider possible ways of improving and extending allied participation in nuclear planning, including improved communications. This is a very interesting suggestion and it was welcomed as deserving further consideration.
In summary, Mr. Speaker, I think the conference was very fruitful. It was in the nature of an experiment, and produced a most worthwhile discussion together with positive results. I would not wish to give the impression that there are no remaining problems, but I do want to emphasize the spirit of co-operation and good will which characterized the meeting. The decisions taken underline the broad areas of agreement in principle and will permit the alliance to continue its important work dedicated to the deterrence of aggres-

NATO-STATEMENT FOLLOWING PARIS MEETING OF DEFENCE MINISTERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the statement made by the Minister is somewhat barren of information. As a matter of fact one could learn a good deal more about what happened at the NATO meeting in Paris by reading the newspapers than by perusing the statement just made by the Minister.
The Minister has told us that there was a divergence of opinion on the matter of strategy. He has not told us what the divergence of opinion was about, or how it was resolved.
He tells the House that a consensus of agreement was reached. I would like to know what that consensus is. It was generally understood that the main divergence of opinion on strategy had to do with whether or not any attack against NATO forces in Europe should be met with either a flexible response or a nuclear response. It has been known for some time that General de Gaulle has been pressing for a nuclear response, whereas a great many of the NATO members -and I certainly share their views-have felt there ought to be a response only in terms of the kind of weapons required to meet the specific situation, that nuclear weapons be held in reserve and conventional weapons used unless it was found absolutely necessary to use nuclear weapons.
This divergence of opinion on strategy between the representatives of the French Republic and other members of NATO is a very clear and important one. How was it resolved? The Minister has not told us. I think the House ought to know. It is certainly important for the people of Canada, and for all members of NATO, to know what the thinking is of the ministers of defence who gathered at that conference.
The other matter which the Minister mentioned briefly, without giving us any information about it, has to do with the diffusion of power with respect to control of nuclear weapons. The Minister tells us that Secretary of Defence McNamara of the United States has suggested that there should be a committee of four or five to study this matter. Mr. Speaker, I am afraid that this suggestion from the U.S. Secretary of Defence is
June 3, 1965	COMMONS
too little and too late. I doubt that this will satisfy France, which has been asking for a long time for a wider framework of consultation, between the members of NATO, with respect to the use of nuclear power.
What are to be the terms of reference of this committee? What nations are going to be represented on this committee? Is its membership to be four or five? What are the Minister's views in respect of this matter? What position did the Canadian Government take when this question was being discussed?
Up to the present time the sole decision on the use of nuclear weapons has lain with the United States as the major nuclear power. Are other nations now to be in a consultative capacity, will they have a veto power, or is the final decision still to remain with the United States? What is the Canadian Government's position on this matter? The Minister does not tell us.
We appreciate the fact that the Minister has made a report to the House, which is an appropriate gesture but, Mr. Speaker, it gives us no information and I hope he will be prepared to give some information to the House at a later stage, either today or on another occasion.

The hon. gentleman referred to a divergence of views. Something has been said on this subject in the papers. But recent reports have indicated there was a closer meeting of minds at Paris on this occasion than there has been in the past-that General de Gaulle has been taking a new look at things, and that compromise was reached on various matters of importance. However, the Minister did not tell us clearly just what did take place in this regard; he indicated only that there was general agreement, more or less. He told the House that this was a very fruit-

NATO Defence Ministers' Meeting ful exchange. As has been pointed out, it does not seem there is very much to substantiate that claim in the report which has just been made to us.
Reference was made to the establishment of force goals. These, it was said, must be more realistic than has been the case in the past. The hon. gentleman went on to tell us that discussion took place regarding a mobile force and that Canada intended to give consideration to this important aspect of defence strategy. We are all in favour of participating in a mobile force of the kind suggested, but we would certainly appreciate more information in this connection.

Mr. Speaker, we too, in this comer of the house, expected a more detailed statement from the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Hellyer), following this conference on the goals of military strategy held in Paris. We find once again that we shall learn a great deal more from the press than we did from the minister.

As a matter of fact, I find it rather strange that we are always siding with the United States, as if we were trying to vie with that gigantic military power. I feel the minister would be much better to direct our military policy to economic problems rather than toward armament, because today all small countries located near large countries turn to economic matters first to feed the hungry before thrusting a bayonet into their face.

Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill is to protect the consumer. It would attach the guarantees and warranties of the original contract to the promissory notes used in these transactions. It is my hope that this will protect the consumer against the dishonest type of company that goes out of business or fails to live up to its contract after selling the promissory note or the negotiable document to another company without there being any of the original protection for that sales contract.

That, in order to secure improved examination of the details of legislation and of public spending, while maintaining the full authority of the House, this House agrees upon the value of making increased use of Standing Committees;
That this House accordingly orders:
1.	(a) That detailed examination of estimates, saving always the right of the Committee of Supply, undertaken by Standing Committees and that not more than 30 days of the time of the House be allocated to the business of supply in each session. For the purpose of this order, the business of supply shall consist of main estimates; interim supply; and supplementary or additional estimates excepting supplementary or additional estimates introduced after the main estimates have been approved, and excepting always the final supplementary or additional estimates;
(b)	That the number of supply motions be reduced from six to four; and
(c)	That a Special Committee of the House, consisting of twenty-four members, to be designated later by the House, be instructed to prepare and to submit to the House forthwith the changes in Standing Orders consequential upon these orders, including any means of giving to the opposition an opportunity to select the departmental estimates to be discussed.
2.	That the Standing Orders be amended by adding thereto a new Standing Order 15-A, to read as follows:
Standing Order 15-A
15-A. (1) There shall be a Business Committee to which the leader of each party in the House from time to time by written notice to the Speaker may appoint one member.
(2)	During routine proceedings a Minister of the Crown may request that the question of allocation of time for consideration of any item of business or stage thereof be referred to the Business Corn-
House of Commons Procedures mittee for consideration and report, and upon such request being made such question shall stand referred to the committee.
(3)	The Business Committee shall report back to the House on or before the third sitting day following such request.
(4)	If the Chairman of the Business Committee reports that the committee has unanimously recommended an allocation of time for the item of business or stage thereof, a Minister of the Crown may without notice propose a motion, to be decided without debate or amendment, for concurrence in the report, and if agreed to, the motion shall have the same effect as if it were an order of the House.
(5)	If the Chairman of the Business Committee reports that the committee has been unable to reach a unanimous agreement or if the committee fails to report within the time specified by Section (3) of this Standing Order, a Minister of the Crown may give notice that at the next sitting of the House he will move that an order be made allocating the time for the item of business or stage thereof.
(6)	A motion of which a Minister has given notice under Section (5) of this Standing Order shall be made during routine proceedings. Unless the debate on the motion has been previously concluded, Mr. Speaker shall at fifteen minutes before the expiry of the time provided for Government business in such sitting interrupt the proceedings and forthwith put every question necessary to dispose of the main motion. A motion requesting allocation of time, if agreed to, shall have the same effect as if it were an order of the House.
(7)	No motion made by a Minister under Sections (5) and (6) of this Standing Order shall provide for the allocation of a period of time shorter than two days for the second reading, two days for the committee stage, and one day for the third reading of any bill. For the purposes of this section, third reading shall be deemed to have been considered for one day provided the order for third reading is called as the first item under Government Orders on a Monday, Tuesday, Thursday or Friday, and provided it is continued, if necessary, until the normal time of adjournment on any such day; provided that if a representative of each party has not spoken, the hour for the adjournment of the sitting shall be extended until a representative of each party has had an opportunity to speak. Such an order having been called on any Monday, Tuesday, Thursday or Friday, it shall have precedence over all other business until the time of adjournment on that day, unless it is disposed of earlier. Under any other circumstances, a total of five hours shall be deemed to be the equivalent of one sitting day.
(8)	During debate on any item of business or stage thereof for which an allocation of time has been made under this Standing Order, if an amendment is proposed which in the opinion of Mr. Speaker materially changes the item of business or stage thereof and which raises any issue for which in the opinion of Mr. Speaker there has not been or otherwise will not be an adequate opportunity for discussion, Mr. Speaker may announce an extension of not more than two days to the allocated period of time.

I would have thought that in view of the serious attempt which has been made on this side of the House to meet the Government in its serious attempt to make alterations in the rules there should be some action on the part of the Prime Minister at this point. The right hon. gentleman introduced this resolution and spoke at length on it. He has manifold duties and apparently he has not delegated authority to his colleagues to respond to suggestions which are made on the floor of the House. We do not particularly wish that this debate should become acrimonious and up to the present time it has been conducted, I think, on a very high level. We responded to the words of the Prime Minister who spoke as follows on May 19:
We think the proposals in the two resolutions are good. They may be better after we have considered the second resolution. There may be amendments made which will improve them.
I pause there for a moment. These amendments, I took it, could be suggested either by the Government side or by the Opposition side. The Prime Minister went on:
But we think they are good. We think they will improve the procedures of the House of Commons and we put them forward for that purpose and for that purpose only and in no partisan spirit.
That was a good level on which to commence this debate. We have responded. We understood that the Prime Minister was speaking to us in good faith. Then on May 27 the Minister of Labour (Mr. MacEachen) said this as reported on page 1727 of Hansard:
The Prime Minister stated yesterday that there was no "take it or leave it" attitude: that the

Government was ready to consider various views which had been put forward by members of the Opposition, views which would have the effect of improving and making more acceptable the resolution which is now before the House.
Again this maintains the standard of debate. This is supposed not to be a partisan issue, a conflict of parties. Members of the House are, together, attempting to make improvements which are desired in the procedures of the House of Commons. The Prime Minister, quoted by the Minister of Labour, said the attitude of the Government was not one of "take it or leave it." We accept those words at their face value and we have made suggestions from this side of the House. Some of those suggestions have been adopted. But it became apparent yesterday that we were becoming deadlocked on the second part of the resolution now before us. This part of the resolution deals with the difficult question of closure.
The suggestion made by my hon. friend from Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) and which I myself made last night was that we should separate the controversial part of this resolution, hold it in abeyance for a while, and deal immediately with that part of the resolution on which there has been substantial agreement-virtually unanimous agreement, I believe. I refer to the part which sets an over-all limitation on the time allotted for a study of the estimates. This was one of the objectives the Government had in mind and it was one of the objectives I put forward in one of the speeches I made on this subject.
The next thing we suggest is connected with the second resolution, which will come before the Committee of the Whole House. We are prepared to pass immediately that portion of it which deals with the renaming of the committees and the allotment of Members to the committees. If these two things were done the House could set up these committees; the estimates which are now before us could be referred to them and the business of the House could be carried on. But if we are going to be confronted with a package deal from the Government side which says, "You must take the whole thing, and take it now, or nothing further will be done", we meet the situation that I mentioned last night where we become deadlocked.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
I thought we were putting forward a very reasonable proposition. It is open to considerable debate whether another form of closure shall be incorporated in our rules, but we are not disposed to continue the

debate with regard to the over-all limitation of time on the estimates or for the reorganization of the committees of the House. The major portion of the changes in the rules proposed by the Government side will prove to be reasonably acceptable to the House. Why should not that major part of the rule changes be immediately put into operation? Why the delay? It is not unusual in this House to have lengthy controversy over certain portions of bills or resolutions. We have valid objections to having another closure rule written into the rule book.
I come back to this, Mr. Speaker. What did the Prime Minister mean by his statement, which was quoted by the Minister of Labour (Mr. MacEachen), "This is not a 'take it or leave it' proposition"? As it stands at the moment, the Government is making it that; it is saying, "Take it, with no substantial changes in this portion of our resolution".

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, let us examine the situation as it now is. During the course of the last ten years we have adopted a program for the allocation of time in respect of certain debates. I had some part in this as a Member of the Committee which studied this matter in 1954-55. We have allocated time in respect of the Speech from the Throne and the budget debate and have substantially reduced the time to be spent in the Committee of the Whole House.
We have now gone even further and will go further yet if we accept the resolution for the allocation of time for the study of the estimates, interim supply and supplementary estimates that come forward during the course of a year. I believe we would be going too far in this regard. All of these allocations of time restrict the activities of Members of the House and reduce their opportunities to speak. Perhaps we should pause at this time in our efforts to allocate the time to be allowed for certain debates rather than adopt this additional restriction which is really another method of closure in respect of legislation.
Assuming that an allocation of time will be adopted in respect of the main estimates, we will then have a limitation on the debate on the Throne Speech of eight days, a limitation on the debate on the budget of six days, a limitation on the debate on supply motions of eight days and a limitation in respect of estimates of 30 days, or a total of 52 sitting days as a maximum for the consideration of that major part of the work of the House. This amounts to about two and a half months, so the Government will have the rest of the year during which to deal with legislation. If we are able to pass the sections which require the extension of hours, and I presume the proposal in that regard will be passed at a later stage, the business of Parliament could be conducted within a five or six month period.
One of the objectives that we have all been thinking about over the years is that Parliament should complete its business in a five or six month period instead of carrying on month after month. Under these arrangements it is within the power of the Government to bring the work of Parliament to a conclusion within six months, making allowances for the odd

House of Commons Procedures day which might be taken up by a special debate or something of that nature. I do not know how much legislation the Government intends to bring in but under these arrangements there would be almost 100 days left for legislative purposes, which is an unusually large amount of time for legislation during the course of a session of Parliament.
As I suggested in a speech I made earlier, within the framework of 150 days we should be able to accomplish the work of Parliament, leaving adequate time for hon. Members to visit their constituencies. My point is that this Government, because of the co-operation of the House generally, has the power to control the length of time that we spend here on the Throne Speech debate, the budget debate, supply motions and estimates. It did not have that power in respect of estimates in the past. Surely that is a sufficient amount of control for the time being. Let us wait for a year or two to see whether under these arrangements the business of the country can be conducted in a satisfactory manner.
I am sure these arrangements will meet the criticism of some Members of the House and uninformed criticism by individuals outside the House. Parliament will not be sitting the year round, but we will be able to get on with the business of the country. I feel that we should now refrain from adopting further limitations or restrictions and avoid the adoption of another closure rule. The part of the resolution we are now considering that is unacceptable is that part which in effect is another closure rule in respect of legislation. Within the other allocations of time there is room for the Opposition to manoeuvre.
On several occasions I have asked that someone tally the number of pieces of legislation passed during the last ten years and the number in respect of which a time limit had to be imposed. No one has taken up that request. Let me point out some statistics in this regard. In 1956 it was considered essential to impose the closure rule in respect of the pipe line debate. Last year it was considered essential to impose this rule in respect of the flag resolution. Those are the two important examples of the last ten years. As I pointed out in an earlier speech, 650 pieces of legislation have been passed by Parliament during the last ten years, most of them without prolonged debate. The kind of legislative items which cause the House to engage in long debates are those which are controversial and also badly drafted bills that have to be revised, of which the pension plan is a good example. The redistribution bill re-

speechtext:
When the hon. lady is examining the record of that House I hope she bears in mind those instances since the war when they imposed a closure method of allocating the time and those instances when they passed certain bills in the Committee of the Whole House without considering at h ast two thirds of the sections of the bills. I am pointing out that is the weakness of the rule we are now attempting to incorporate here in the House of Commons.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
We should study the good points and the bad points of British practice. As I read the British Hansard, they consider their allocation of time practice with regard to bills is a bad one. As I mentioned before, they apologize when they introduce it. The apology of a Government Member introducing a bill is different from the apology of anyone else, of course, but they do apologize for introducing it. There is a lengthy debate for a whole day with everyone talking about how bad it is to do it this way, and only a Government intent upon forcing its will upon the people goes through with it. I doubt very much whether that practice in England, which has been decreasing over the last 10 years, will continue without considerable modification.
I say, let us not introduce here a second closure method on legislation, the necessity for which has not been proven because legislation has gone through this House very rapidly. If controversial legislation is brought in, the Government should accept a lengthy debate so that the people of this country will know what is going on. Despite the rapidity of our communications and the effectiveness of our mass media, it does take several days before controversial items discussed in this House of Commons reach the people. We have discovered that from our experience on both sides of the House. But after the lapse of a few days of spirited debate in the House

and attention by the Press Gallery and comments by editors of newspapers the public then becomes informed about what is going on. The danger is that if there is another closure imposed on legislation that type of information to the public will be denied and things might be forced through this House which should not be forced through. There is always a value in sober second thought in this chamber as well as in the other.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to take this opportunity to make a few remarks in this important debate and to reply in brief to the suggestion made by the hon. Member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill).
We are now entering upon the ninth full day of this debate on the resolutions introduced by the Government in order to improve the procedures of the House. During this time many Members from all parties have been heard and some Members have been heard twice. I believe that thorough and detailed examination has been given to the first resolution.
Some changes or modifications in the Government's proposals have been suggested during this debate. The Government has acknowledged the value of these suggestions
June 3, 1965

and has acceded to every reasonable amendment which has been suggested both as to the procedure tor supply debates and as to the procedure for programming the business of the House.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR CONSIDERATION OF ESTIMATES AND ALLOCATION OF TIME

speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio; Solicitor General of Canada

At the suggestion of
several Members we have modified the proposals concerning supply debates. We have changed the number of supply motions from six to four; we have separated the period for debate on the supply motions from the period to be fixed for debate on supply generally; we have removed from the period fixed for supply debates the supplementary estimates introduced after the main estimates have been considered; and we have removed the final supplementary estimates.
The effect of these changes, Mr. Speaker, has been to extend the period which was originally proposed for supply debates from 36 to 40 days and in some circumstances to an even longer period. We have even acceded to a request to change the size of the proposed Special Committee which is to draft the resulting Standing Orders.
We have also provided the safeguard that Members have sought concerning the proposed Standing Order 15A, which provides a method for programming the business of the House. It was suggested that a Government might be able to introduce a major amendment at the end of the period of time fixed for debate on a particular measure. To prevent this possibility we provided an amendment allowing the Speaker to extend the allotted period of time to enable Members to examine any last minute amendment so made. It was suggested further that an allotted time period might be so short as to curb debate unduly.

I believe that that amendment was made late one evening just before the ten o'clock adjournment. I want to stress at this time that this suggestion concerning the length of Members' speeches was not made by the Government. The Government's proposals were not intended in any way to restrict full and free debate by Members. What they were intended to do was to ensure that representatives of all parties should meet to plan and program a reasonable length of time for the major measures that come before the House. We believe that the worst restriction on the freedom of speech is the use of debating techniques which oblige the House to continue debating a measure long after every possible opinion or shade of opinion has been expressed-

Perhaps most important of all, the Government has been prepared to modify its proposal that the changes be made permanent and has offered an amendment to provide for the changes to be on a trial basis until the end of the next session. This will ensure that after a fair trial the proposed changes can be re-examined by the House.
A recent proposal-I refer to the proposal made by the hon. Member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill)-was that the Government should split the resolution now before us, carve out part of another resolution which is to come before us and submit this to the House. I believe, Mr. Speaker, that this suggestion that supply procedure and the committee structure should be divorced from other governmental procedural proposals is quite unrealistic. I believe the fixing of a stated length of time for debating supply motions and for debating supply is a most important aspect of programming House business and should not be divorced from other Government proposals for a system of programming House business.
Now that we have given full and complete consideration to the first resolution, may I appeal to all hon. Members to allow the proposals as modified to come before us for a vote? If accepted by the House they could be instituted on a trial basis. Unduly delaying reform of our procedures cannot help but destroy the esteem and value of our Parliamentary institutions.

I want to say that what I am about to say is my own opinion and not necessarily the opinion of anyone else. I have been interested in the remarks made by the previous speaker concerning how much the Government has been willing to amend its proposals. Hon. Members will recall a committee was set up

to discuss these proposals and the Government rejected its report. The Government brought before Parliament its own proposals which were very far reaching and in my opinion not too clearly thought out.

speechtext: No, of course not, but the committee proposals were rounded out to take into consideration a number of things. This is my point. I think hon. Members should be interested in taking a look at themselves during the last few days. We are stalling for some reason or other, and I wonder-

maintopic: PROVISION FOR CONSIDERATION OF ESTIMATES AND ALLOCATION OF TIME

maintopic: PROVISION FOR CONSIDERATION OF ESTIMATES AND ALLOCATION OF TIME
speechtext: We have no proper agenda before us. The Government's agenda appeared in the Throne Speech but that was a political document for an election which was expected early in the spring. The election has not occurred and is not going to occur in June so that Throne Speech is no longer of any value. There is no agenda before Parliament. We do not know really what faces us in the form of legislation and yet we are being asked to take care of some eventuality the Government thinks might develop when they would want to use the guillotine. Since I have been a Member, and it is not very long-

speechtext:
It may be too long for some people but they will learn after they have been here for a period of time-one of the things I have been able to learn is that it is increasingly difficult for the individual Member to represent his riding. There is a great tendency in this House to establish political parties and give these parties complete control over most operations that are of interest to the private Member. Since 1957 we have made a number of attempts to correct some of these problems. We have agreed that in those formal debates in which the backbencher has an opportunity to represent his riding there shall be a limitation of debate. We reduced the debate on the Throne Speech, a formal debate in which the backbencher can participate,
House of Commons Procedures from ten days to eight days. Prior to that the debate on the Throne Speech was unlimited and could continue as long as any backbencher wanted to speak. The next formal debates we have are the supply debates. Since I became a Member of the House these have been reduced from eight to six days and there has been a technical agreement that they will be further reduced to four.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
I have no argument with the fact that in the formal debates which we have, arrangements have been arrived at in most cases. I have gone into the history of the External Affairs debates, which are normally asked for by the Opposition and are granted on the basis of a two day debate. When this occurs the first round of formal debate is occupied by the leader or official spokesman for each political party in the House.
The second round of debate is usually occupied by three Government supporters, three members of the Official Opposition, and one Member of each of the other parties in the House. I have known of no more than five hon. Members taking part in the first day of debate, which on occasion has been abused by one or two speakers occupying most of the time, but on no occasion is there time for more than two speakers from any of the other parties in the House.
This is what we are doing now with the guillotine motion and the reference to the Business Committee. We are allowing the political parties to become the functioning part of Parliament and are taking away from each individual Member his fundamental right to represent his riding because we are allowing the parties to decide how long a debate should take and who should speak in it.
Maybe one cannot fight change or tradition but I think change should come about by agreement. In my view the one time the guillotine motion could have been introduced with complete justification was during the flag debate. There are some who will disagree with this. I violently oppose closure in the context in which we have had it but I see the guillotine motion in a different light. The closure motion has a bad connotation throughout the country and very few people agree to the use of it. But if we had a guillotine motion that operated in a milder way no responsible Member of the House would be prepared to oppose it. Only two or three debates have taken place since 1957 which would have warranted the use of the guillotine.

It could have been used because of repetition in the Throne Speech debate or because of filibuster but now the backbenchers are being asked to allow the Business Committee exactly the same power as the Government has under the existing closure provision. We are being asked to allow the political parties to decide who shall speak, how long a debate shall continue and, by agreement, what Members may rise in their places and speak on behalf of their constituents on a matter on which they have completely contrary views to the positions taken by their respective parties.
Maybe people do not care about this but I do. In many respects I have been a fairly free thinker for a long time. I came to Parliament to represent the people of Timiskaming. This has nothing to do with my political philosophy and I want the opportunity to represent my constituents. If we pass this resolution without any justification for it, then we are really saying to the backbencher, "You have no role; the only role in this House is that occupied by political parties".
Some hon. Members who support the Government have objected to the resolution. I have always said that Government backbenchers in Parliament are not treated fairly. They are only rubber stamps. If they dare to oppose then they receive no party contributions at election time and their only alternative is to run as independents. This is a political fact of life in Canada. I have been interested to see some of them exert themselves, and I think they should not be stupid enough to eliminate the right they now have by giving it to a Business Committee which will allocate the time they can have.
Some hon. Members may want to take this right away. There are some who do not care to make speeches on behalf of their constituents. They find they can represent them in other ways. That is all well and good. That is the choice they make, but if the new backbencher does not stand up and make his contribution, if he does not decide what niche he should occupy in order to give his constituency the best representation possible, then he will not be returned at the next election. I do not believe we should take away this right from the backbencher.
I am in complete agreement that we have to make some changes. I believe that with co-operation the length of time spent on estimates will not exceed the limit proposed. I believe the House committees can serve a useful function but if they are to do so this

DEBATES	June 3, 1965
year they should be set up as soon as possible.
There is some legitimate argument in favour of asking for the provision of a guillotine motion but not before the crime is committed. I remember one time during a strike there was some difficulty on the picket line and a certain amount of violence. I had to raise a large amount of bail money. I had to have houses pledged and go through quite a process in order to raise bail and I asked myself why not raise bail money before other offences take place inasmuch as I anticipated that other such occasions might arise. But when I told our union lawyer I had already pledged about $1J million worth of property for offences that might happen in the future he pretty nearly went through the roof because one is not supposed to do this sort of thing.
Likewise I say the Government should not ask Parliament to give away fundamental rights and make such decisions before it is necessary to do so. If changes are necessary we should make them, but there is no one in the country who will not agree that the first thing that must be done is that the Government has to be fair to Parliament, tell us what the timetable is going to be, what legislation we are going to have, and set it forth in an order of priority. However, this is not being done.
We are being asked to allot time. We are being asked to restrict the length of speeches. We are being asked to eliminate the backbencher in a political party. Probably there is a better way to put that. We are being asked to prevent a nonconformist Member of a political party from having his say if his party does not wish him to speak.
The last speaker got up and said, "We made concessions". I am damned if they made concessions. They made proposals and only agreed to concessions sought by others. It is not my job to make such proposals. They say they need these changes in order to conduct the business of the House better, and there are too many people in the House willing to co-operate with them.
I do not really believe these changes can be stopped. There are many Members who are as convinced as I am that the rules have to be used to solve our problem, a problem that is faced in pretty nearly every democratic country in the world. We are trying to use the rules to make Parliament mere effective. Almost every country in the world has the same problem and has examined every possible means in order to find a solution for it. However, I think that before
June 3, 1965

a backbencher, on the Government side or elsewhere, says "me too" in agreement with the proposed changes, he should think seriously about them.
I have heard some hon. Members say, "I am not going to run again; I am going to go back home and run my farm or business". The only reason they do not intend to run for Parliament is that they do not participate in its functioning and cannot find a way to participate. If they give away the little rights that remain to them they will find themselves more and more unable to participate.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
Since I have been here sessions have become longer and longer despite the fact that we have curtailed the formal debates. In the past ten years, for instance, the right of unlimited debate on the Address has been abolished. I do not think this has led to any real reduction in the length of our sessions. It must be remembered that both the gross national product and tax revenues have been increasing rapidly. We say we are increasing our ability to examine estimates inasmuch as we are reducing debates on supply motions by allowing four days instead of eight. I predict that before a year or two has passed we shall get rid of supply motions altogether with the exception of the introductory motion.
It seems to me Parliament should consider what it really wishes to do. If it really wishes to make changes in the rules it will have to prepare a parliamentary timetable. No one in his senses would object to this. There is no organization similar in size to this one which operates without a formal agenda. There is no municipal council which starts out without an agenda. We have abused the Speech from the Throne until it has become little more than a political document. Half the items which appear in it appeared in it 15 years ago. It is kept shiny for election purposes. There is an obligation upon the Government to prepare an agenda. There is an obligation to face the question of the private Members' hour. There may be reason to consider the question of the Speaker's office. The Internal Economy Commission-once I referred to it as the Eternal Economy Commission and that might have been a better description-has miserably failed to do the job allotted to it. Nowhere else, so far as I have been able to discover, is the Government charged with authority in this field. In other places this task is given to Members of the Commons with representation from the Treasury Benches.

If this motion passes as amended we shall in effect have applied a closure motion to the second part besides imposing certain conditions with which no one but a barbarian would agree. The Federal Parliament devotes attention to ensuring certain standards of employment in areas not directly related to the work of Parliament. Yet if these proposals go through it will mean treating in barbarous fashion the people who work directly for us, the people over whom we have direct control.
I say that if we pass this resolution we shall have eliminated for all time the right to engage in protracted debate when serious questions arise. Consider the problem which is developing with regard to our constitution. Is the Official Opposition prepared to say now that they are ready to accept limitation of debate on that subject, knowing that such a discussion can be concluded whenever a Minister of the Crown feels it should be concluded? If they are saying that, then let us have the election now. I think the Official Opposition will really not be the same after the election.
The question of changes is a most important one, though the majority of Members opposite with whom I discuss it appear not to understand what is involved in the proposals for rule changes. These resolutions would give the Government authority to make decisions affecting the operation of Parliament itself and before they are adopted the whole question should be considered seriously in a committee of the House where all aspects could be discussed and where counter-proposals could be made in a more effective manner than by proposing amendments.
The suggestion made by the hon. Member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill) is not an unreasonable one. He offered to accept certain proposals of the Government as amended, together with the recommendation for the establishment of committees so that these committees could begin their work. Then the other questions left over from item 14 and those contained in item 15 on the order paper could be studied in toto. No one would disagree that these resolutions are directly related; if one is passed, the other might be hard to change. I hope all Members, particularly those backbenchers who have spoken so eloquently in favour of reform, will look forward to the day when we have a proper agenda in this House so that each of us may know what the Government proposes to do from day to day, to the end that preparations can be made before measures are brought forward on the floor of the House.

I would add a postscript which has just occurred to me. It has to do with the resolution stage. It is often forgotten how much co-operation has been extended to this Government in carrying out desired changes. For instance, we did reach agreement that the resolution stage preceding a bill should be limited on a trial basis to one day. What we were saying in effect was this: That the resolution stage was of no value, that the bill should be drafted and prepared for introduction, that only pious speeches would be made on the resolution stage and that the main discussion should take place on the bill itself.
I would point out, however, that when resolutions involving the expenditure of money were first introduced in the parliamentary system the resolution stage was the stage at which every Member gave his views on the subject. The Government then decided to develop its legislation on the basis of the views expressed so that the bill when produced represented the majority opinion of those interested. In agreeing to give up the resolution stage we were, in effect, giving up the right to have any say in what the legislation should be except for the doubtful expedient of moving amendments later to something which had already been set out in a definite form. This right to move amendments to something which has already been put forward is a far cry from being able to contribute to the original presentation. These proposals now before us were not arrived at by agreement. The amendments made to them represent concessions on the part of the Government, and I think this is putting things "ass backwards", to use my vernacular. We should have started in committee and held these discussions beforehand.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
I know that the House Leader is sincerely interested in making rule changes that will work. I am aware that this is his motive and it is a very sincere one. I also think he will not disagree with me when I say that overriding this is the Government's desire to get business done the way it wants it done.
In a democracy and in a House that in my opinion is going to be composed of minorities for some years to come, consideration really will have to be given to our changing complex and we will have to arrive at rule changes that can be agreed upon, supported and sincerely put into practice by every Member in this House. If anything less is accomplished, Mr. Speaker, I predict that

there will be a very much lesser saving of time than is forecast.

Mr. Speaker, when the hon. Member for Timis-kaming (Mr. Peters) rose to speak he said he did not necessarily expect any other Member to agree entirely with what he was going to say. This does not mean that so far as I am concerned there is not a good deal of food for thought in regard to a number of things said by the hon. Member for Timiskaming. I have considered rather carefully the proposal put forward by the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Mcllraith) in respect of a motion he was prepared to move if the amendment and subamendment before us were withdrawn. So far as I am concerned, Mr. Speaker, I am prepared to support that particular proposal if it becomes a motion before the House. But I do think recognition should be given to a couple of points made by the hon. Member for Timiskaming.
I think one is that while the proposed time allocation committee or Business Committee representing the parties in the House may very well be a proper step leading to the organization of the business of the House, nevertheless it is still as it stands only a part of the required steps that are needed. I agree with the Member for Timiskaming that if this proposal is to mean what some of us hope it will mean, there has to be coupled with it what the Member for Timiskaming described as an agenda for each session of any particular Parliament. The proposal the Government has put forward in the second part of Order No. 14, which we are now debating, is confined to a particular item of business. I am referring to the proposed Standing Order 15A. Unless that is put in the context of considering the business of a session as a whole I am inclined to agree that the Member for Timiskaming has a good point when he suggests there is going to be a breakdown in the effectiveness of this proposal.
The second point made by the hon. Member for Timiskaming to which I think more attention should be given and upon which there should be some further clarification is with regard to the proposal for time allocation as it affects the basic right of an individual, private Member of this House to have an opportunity to speak before debate is con-
June 3, 1965

eluded if he so desires. This point has been referred to not only by the Member for Timiskaming but by a number of other hon. Members on both sides of the House and it is one we should not lose sight of. The following appears in paragraph (7) of proposed Standing Order 15A with regard to the adjournment hour being extended:
-provided that if a representative of each party has not spoken, the hour for the adjournment of the sitting shall be extended until a representative of each party has had an opportunity to speak.
That arrangement was perhaps agreed to rather hastily and without giving due consideration to the point made by the Member for Timiskaming and a number of other Members, namely, that before debate is concluded a Member should have an opportunity, if he feels impelled to do so, to express his views in the House on behalf of his constituents. With regard to this point I have reason to agree with the Member for Timiskaming and the ideas expressed by quite a number of other Members. If at any stage of the proceedings with regard to a particular bill or piece of business in a debate under a time allocation order Members desiring to speak have not spoken by the normal adjournment hour of the House, the normal hour of adjournment should be suspended, as I believe one Member put it, to a time not later than the time set for the next sitting of the House.
All hon. Members will realize that this might involve the House sitting all through the night or on into the wee, small, hours of the morning, but I would suggest that in its practical application it is a rule that is not very likely to be abused too often by Members of the House if it is put into eifect. I should like to say that in addition to accepting the proposal put forward by the President of the Privy Council, which it has been indicated the Members of this party by and large are prepared to accept and so will agree to withdraw the amendment proposed by the hon. Member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin), we should have an indication from the President of the Privy Council that there would be this kind of extension of the normal sitting hours with respect to a debate in progress under a time allocation order. We should also have a firmer indication from the President of the Privy Council- than we have so far had from him or the Prime Minister in respect of laying out a normal "timetable for the sittings of Parliament. When I say "normal timetable", I recognize that if any such proposal were to be translated into the Standing Orders of the House

provision would have to be made whereby if the Government deemed it necessary to deal with an emergency or some very urgent public business this rule could from time to time be altered. Unless those two points are covered, Mr. Speaker, I for one believe that some of the dangers mentioned by the hon. Member for Timiskaming will in fact occur, and they are dangers that should not be disregarded by the general membership of the House.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the House is aware the Government has been reviewing its policy with respect to the export of uranium.
World requirements for uranium for peaceful purposes will increase very greatly in the years to come. Canada holds a substantial portion of the known uranium reserves of the world and in the future may well be the largest single supplier for the rest of the world. It is vital that the Canadian industry be in the best possible position to take advantage of expanding markets for the peaceful uses of this commodity.
As one part of its policy to promote the use of Canadian uranium for peaceful purposes the Government has decided that export permits will be granted, or commitments to issue export permits will be given, with respect to sales of uranium covered by contracts entered into from now on, only if the uranium is to be used for peaceful purposes. Before such sales to any destination are authorized, the Government will require an agreement with the government of the importing country to ensure with appropriate verification and control, that the uranium is to be used for peaceful purposes only.
Canada has been a member of the International Atomic Energy Agency since its inception and successive governments have vigorously supported the principle of safeguards
June 3, 1965

on uranium sales. This policy is a fudamental part of Canada's general policy to work internationally to avoid the proliferation of nuclear weapons.
As to the commercial aspects of the policy, two general principles will apply, designed to facilitate exports and to ensure that the requirements of both export and domestic consumers are met in an orderly way.
First, the Government recognizes that countries constructing or planning to construct nuclear reactors will wish to make long term arrangements for fuel supply. Accordingly, the Government will be prepared to authorize forward commitments by Canadian producers to supply reactors which are already in operation, under construction, or committed for construction in other countries for the average anticipated life of each reactor, generally calculated for amortization purposes to be 30 years.
Second, and in addition, the Government will be prepared to authorize the export for periods of up to five years of reasonable quantities of uranium for the accumulation of stocks in the importing country.
Within the terms of the policy I have outlined, the Canadian Government will actively encourage and assist the Canadian uranium industry in seeking export markets. The commercial aspects of the policy will, of course, be reviewed from time to time in the light of changing conditions.
Finally, in order to avoid any reduction in the current level of employment and production in the industry in Canada, the Government will purchase uranium for stockpiling to the extent that current sales prove insufficient to achieve this objective during the next five years. These purchases will be made at a price of $4.90 per pound of uranium oxide. Purchases will be made only from companies which have previously produced uranium and will be limited, in the case of each company willing to sell at $4.90, to the amount necessary to maintain an appropriate minimum level of employment and production for that company.
As soon as the details of the stockpiling program, including arrangements for eventual disposal, have been discussed with the uranium industry and decided upon they will be announced to the House and Parliament will be asked to approve the necessary expenditure for the current fiscal year.
Right Hon, J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition): Mr. Speaker, the statement
22620-125}
Policy on Uranium Exports made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) is in rather general terms in that it fails to outline, even in a general way, the degree to which inspection will be required and be mandatory to assure the uses of uranium being confined to peaceful purposes.
As this is a change in the procedure that has been followed over the years with the United States and Great Britain, I hope there was full consultation on it with those two countries. Otherwise it will have the appearance of simply being a means to get around the difficulties now being experienced in assuring uranium sales to the Republic of France. We should know what are the bases upon which inspection will be assured and maintained so that the pledged word will indeed be carried out.
As to the problem with regard to particular communities, I would hope that Faraday Mines would receive consideration now and that that area would not be among those areas that no longer are regarded as productive of uranium.
I am glad to hear that in the years ahead it will be ultimately assured that Canada will continue to be one of the major producers. I am not so sure that that hope is justified on the basis of the limited knowledge I have of the subject, because certainly uranium is found in various parts of the world.
Indeed, as I listened to the Prime Minister making his statement I was reminded of the changes that can take place over the years. As I recall it, the 1920 edition of the Encyclopedia Britannica said in effect that uranium was a yellow mineral without value. The technological changes and scientific developments of the intervening years have greatly altered the opinions of 45 years ago.
I hope, whatever the monetary advantages this change of policy may have and whatever contracts may be entered into hereafter with countries purchasing uranium, that Canada's position will not be uncertain and that we will insist on the right of inspection within the countries making the purchases.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think we would want time to study the full implications of the Prime Minister's statement. I gather from the remarks he has made that from now on export permits will be granted only with respect to uranium which is to be used for peaceful purposes.
My understanding is that up until now the United States and Great Britain have been free from this restriction. I hope that tomor-
June 3. 1965

Policy on Uranium Exports row during question period or at another early date the Prime Minister will clarify whether his announcement of today means that from henceforth Great Britain and the United States will also be required to certify that any uranium which is purchased from Canada will be used solely for peaceful purposes.
The other question on which I should like clarification at an early date concerns the statement that the Government will require an agreement with the Government of the importing country to ensure that the uranium is to be used for peaceful purposes only. Provision is to be made for verification and control. Does "verification" include inspection or is it merely to consist of a document of certification from the Government of the importing country? I think those points should be clarified. I certainly wish to commend the Government for its announcement, meaning as I hope it does that Canada intends to be very strict about ensuring that from now on any uranium exported from this country will be subject to inspection and control to make absolutely sure it will be used only for peaceful purposes.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
The second point in the Prime Minister's statement has to do with stockpiling of uranium pending the time there will be a greater demand for this important commodity. I believe the Government is making a wise move in this regard. All the indications are that the demand for uranium will increase tremendously in the next few years. A great many nuclear reactor plants are being built in various parts of the world and it is estimated that by 1973 there will be a very large demand for uranium, one which Canada will be called upon to fill to a large extent because other sources of uranium are not as extensive as ours with the exception of those in the former Belgian Congo. I think we are wise to keep the industry viable by accepting uranium, paying a guaranteed price and stockpiling it against the demand which is almost certain to come.
However, there are one or two points on which we would like clarification. Is the price of $4.90 to be a flexible price? If the world price rises or falls from time to time will the price paid for stockpiling vary correspondingly?

subtopic: CONDITIONS APPLICABLE TO GRANTING OF EXPORT PERMITS-STOCKPILING PROGRAM
speechtext: It is the stockpiling price.

subtopic: CONDITIONS APPLICABLE TO GRANTING OF EXPORT PERMITS-STOCKPILING PROGRAM
speechtext:
Someone says it is the stockpiling price. It is, I assume, the price which

will be paid by the Government for uranium for stockpiling. Does this mean that if there is an increase in the price, for example, the increase would go to those who produce the uranium? If it is based on arrangements similar to those by which we purchase wheat through the Wheat Board which involve a guaranteed price, then any subsequent increase would be passed on to the producer.
I think that is sensible.
There is a further point I wish to raise. Has the Government discussed this arrangement with other uranium producing countries to ascertain whether there might be some agreement between importing and exporting countries with regard to the price range in very much the same way as has been done under the international wheat agreement? It appears to me that negotiations of this kind would be exceedingly useful since they might lead to avoidance of the wide fluctuations in price which would otherwise take place. When the new reactors are in operation there is likely to be a sudden demand for uranium which could result in a great deal of speculation on the market. If some agreement could be reached between exporting and importing countries on a price range it seems to me this would bring stability to the uranium market and help to do what the Government has in mind, namely, to maintain employment and production in the uranium industry.

subtopic: CONDITIONS APPLICABLE TO GRANTING OF EXPORT PERMITS-STOCKPILING PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this announcement is certainly one of great interest not only to Members of this House but to the entire uranium industry in Canada. In the last few weeks Canadian policy with regard to uranium has evidently appeared hypocritical. The Government has been negotiating the sale of uranium in Paris, such sale to be dependent on a guarantee that the uranium would be used only for peaceful purposes, while being committed at the same time to selling uranium to Great Britain and the United States on a basis which provides no restriction whatsoever. I think the Government should be commended on applying a consistent policy so far as the markets for our uranium are concerned.
I question the value of investigation and control apart from the guarantees given by the countries which purchase the uranium. After all, Canada is not the only source of uranium and until every exporting country agrees that the uranium it sells must not be used except for peaceful purposes the reservations which the Prime Minister has men-
June 3. 1965

tioned will only mean that that part of the uranium supply that comes from Canada will be used for peaceful purposes while the other part, which does not carry such a restriction, will be used for different purposes. Since Canada has taken the lead in this direction it is only logical to pursue vigorously the establishment of an agreement of some kind between ourselves and the other suppliers of uranium so that effective control may be imposed on the use of uranium.
The policy of stockpiling which the Government has announced is, I believe, a sound one. As has been mentioned, there is a tremendous potential market for uranium in the years ahead, ot only for the generation of electricity but for all other peaceful purposes. We expect to hear more with regard to price. While it is essential to establish a fixed price for stockpiling, market conditions can change and I trust the policy which has been announced will be flexible enough to meet such changes. I believe the Government was right in formulating its present policy, particularly while it is negotiating with France for the sale of a large quantity of uranium. I believe this policy will be accepted favourably in other parts of the world. It is certainly aimed at some degree of international control so that nuclear power may be used for the purposes for which we all believe it should be used, that is, for peaceful purposes only.

subtopic: CONDITIONS APPLICABLE TO GRANTING OF EXPORT PERMITS-STOCKPILING PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
I should like to join with previous speakers to commend the government for having sought and apparently found a formula which will permit Canada to become one of the leading exporting countries for such an important product as uranium. I understand that the strict agreements concluded, especially during the negotiations with France, may have represented for Canada an obstacle for the export of this raw material which is in great demand, as far as the sale of part of the Canadian production of uranium is concerned.
The policy just announced by the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) will surely please all hon. members. However, that policy should not be fully accepted before certain questions are answered regarding, for instance, the inspection and control to be exercised by the Canadian government on the use of uranium because France will surely not be the only eventual outlet, for I am under the impression that we will also be getting orders from countries such as Communist China and

House of Commons Procedures Russia who may become customers of Canada in that field.
Mr. Speaker, it is to be hoped that the inspection and control formula for the use of uranium exported from Canada will also prompt other countries to agree to and accept that formula which would provide for adequate inspection and efficient control and ensure the peaceful use of uranium.
Like all hon. members, we are happy to see that a way has been found to give new life to the uranium industry by making easier the sale of as much of that raw material as possible for peaceful purposes.
