speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am not moved by groans on the part of hon. Members over there.
I do not know how many meetings of the Special Committee on Procedure and Organization of this House I attended, but I am not moved to worry about the fact that this is the ninth day of debate on rule changes because this could and might be a crucial time in respect of the procedural affairs of this Parliament.
House of Commons Procedures I should like to commence my remarks by quoting from, of all people, a group of Conservatives. I want to remind the Government of what the authors of "Change or Decay: Parliament and Government in our Industrial Society" say about Bagehot as being a legend. The authors were a group of Conservative Members of Parliament in Britain and they wrote this pamphlet in 1963. They quote Bagehot as saying, and I think we should all consider this sentence: "The very means which best helped you yesterday may very likely be those which most impede you tomorrow." I think that we sitting to your left, Sir, should also take this advice because, after all, that is what Parliament is all about. We should not be ashamed of this because it is the basis of Parliament.
Professor Denis Smith, in his paper prepared for the Special Committee on Procedure and Organization, wrote:
The argument from tradition has strength: it suggests caution in the application of parliamentary reform, to ensure that valuable features of the parliamentary system will not be lost unwittingly in the pursuit of change. But Parliament is not an institution based upon an unchangeable or logical pattern. It is full of incongruities that exist because they work. The test for parliamentary devices should be whether they actually achieve what they are meant to achieve: if they do not, then other devices may legitimately be adopted. [DOT] (8:10 p.m.)
It is in this context that I want to say a word or two to the House.
Parliament is 760 years old this year, and in this country and in the United Kingdom thoughtful people seek methods for improving its work habits. I am not one of those who are too troubled about the amount of talk concerning Parliament or its Members. I think this is a healthy sign because these are days when techniques and systems and beliefs are undergoing searching examination to see if they meet the standards that this age requires of them.
I have in my hand a pamphlet issued by the Royal Bank of Canada, the Monthly Letter for December, 1964, from which I should like to quote a paragraph or two. The pamphlet is entitled "Parliament Is 700 Years Old". The following appears in the pamphlet:
Recalling how ancient empires lost their hard won freedom by listlessness, George Hambleton wrote in 1951: "To stand still is to retreat. And, if we retreat, weak and irresolute Parliaments will again give rise to oligarchic forms of government, little removed from the tyrannies of medieval kings."
Today's outburst of public demonstrations in many countries is an evidence of anti-parliamentarianism. Here are people who care passionately about affairs ranging from the nuclear bomb through racial

June 3, 1965
House of Commons Procedures equality to parish problems who have no confidence in the efficacy of political action. By their parades and displays they are really expressing a profound subconscious defeatism about their own ability to influence events.
The task of Parliament is to identify the problems of society, to evolve policies from ideas, and to carry through the necessary action programs.
Having said that mouthful we must remember-I think many speakers have said this but in different words from mine-that we are not running a business enterprise here. We are not managers or executives or directors. We are, if nothing else, and I say this with all diffidence, specialists in the art of conciliation of differing ideals and interests. It seems to me that if we seek to conciliate different ideals and interests we must employ if we can the qualities of openmindedness and reasonableness. I am one of those who believe that these qualities are sharpened by active use.
Bernard Crick, in an article in the Observer of May 2 this year, wrote:
Few doubt that by and large Parliament raises the right issues, but does anyone believe that its facilities and procedures throw much light on them? Parliament fails in its task of scrutinizing the administration because both M.P.'s and public still believe the myth that Parliament's main function is to turn out Governments, and are still hypnotized by legislation.
Mr. Crick says that M.P.'s need to emancipate themselves from the bygone days when the division lobby was held to be the true instrument of parliamentary control. He says that just about half of Parliament's time-he is referring, of course, to the United Kingdom -is consumed by the great god legislation, who gets his way anyway. And legislation is drafted in ridiculous detail by Parliament. He ends his exhortation by saying:
But far too little time is spent in scrutiny and investigation.
I do not want to step over into the next resolution too much, Mr. Speaker, although I note from reading the debate that even the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) saw fit to encompass in his address both items. But I am one who believes that the parliamentary system should do much more scrutinizing than the present system envisages or even the system proposed by the Government. I think it is a pity that the suggestions made by the Special Committee on Procedure and Organization were not adopted because they were more far reaching in this regard than are the somewhat timid suggestions of the Government.
The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefen-baker) rightly deplored absenteeism in the

House. I know a good many of my fellow Members are taking part tonight in a public panel on the abolition of the death penalty, which is a responsibility of theirs, and of course cannot be here. But I am going to have the temerity as a comparatively new backbencher to suggest that there are one or two reasons for absenteeism. One of them is boredom. Second-this was also mentioned by my hon. friend from Queens-there is the lack of a definite term for Parliament with fixed periods of adjournment.
When we speak of absenteeism we must not fall into the habit of some of our newspaper editorials lately in making what I think is a fetish out of attendance in Parliament. They look through long lists and ask where certain Members were, why they did not vote and so on. I think a Member is more than one who can bend his back behind a seat in this Parliament. If a Member is to fulfil his proper functions in this country he must be part of the very life of the country, taking part in all sorts of activities whether they are in his constituency or taking place in any other part of the country.
In another section of the Royal Bank Monthly Letter the author reminds us that one of the great functions of a Member of Parliament is that of being an instrument of education. How many people in this Parliament can be an instrument of education if they are tied to a set routine in a Parliament which sits far too long?
I suppose any of us could catalogue a list of reasons for boredom. If I were asked for mine, one of them would be long and repetitious speeches, another, too lengthy periods of time on relatively unimportant bits of legislation, and yet a third, too much detailed consideration of spending estimates by the Committee of Supply. Some of these abuses of privilege will be curtailed by the rule changes we are now considering.
I believe with all respect that the Speaker should enforce the rule against repetition of a point which has already been made. Merely repeating a point of view does not serve to reinforce an argument; it merely serves, in my humble opinion, to stupefy those who have to listen. I believe too that Members of Parliament should be asked to serve on Government inquiries and commissions. I do not mean automatic membership for Members according to any party ratio, but when we subtract the obviously ineligible Cabinet Ministers and their Parliamentary Secretaries from our number, surely among the rest of us one or two could be found who could give
June 3, 1985

useful service. I think, for example, of the new Special Committee on Correction under the Minister of Justice (Mr. Favreau). I mention that not through any wish to single out the Minister of Justice but merely as an example which comes to mind as a result of the announcement made yesterday. Too little use is made in Parliament of committees of inquiry and of outside advisory committees to the Government.
[DOT] (8:20 p.m.)
In Bernard Crick's book on the reform of Parliament he gives a list of the various commissions and other forms of inquiry in Britain for a period of some 50 years. The sad thing is that it is a rare occasion upon which a Member of Parliament is asked to be part of any such inquiry. I think this action serves to isolate a Member from some of the thoughtful activities going on in the country. I do not believe there is any partisan aspect, for instance, to a committee on corrections. I do not think there is a Conservative, Socialist or Social Credit attitude toward the reform of prisoners. I think somewhere in this place there are people who could give useful service.
Edmund Burke once said that one must reform in order to preserve. Well, it is a good thing for a Tory like me to quote one of the great Tories. But then I have to balance this with the question that Hazlitt asked when he wrote an essay on Edmund Burke and said, "Preserve what?". I suppose that is what we are about in this nine or ten day debate. Bernard Crick, who by the way was at Couchiching last year during the seminar that was held by the Canadian Institute of Public Affairs and the C.B.C. on Parliament and some of the problems faced by Parliament, reminds us he is very serious in thinking there had better be some real effort at reform, for there is ample evidence from the history of our times and general grounds in political and social theory for believing that the strongest-seeming free systems of Government can crumble from within if the masses cease to understand or care how they are governed and begin to think that attempts to control or influence Government are all a farce and a racket anyway.
I do not believe, in the last few short years of my experience here, that anything has troubled me more than the question of the general public. I agree with the hon. Member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill) when he says that in many instances public opinion is ill informed. However, I
House of Commons Procedures suggest it is ill informed because we have not done our job. We Members of Parliament have not informed the public. This is one of our major responsibilities.
Some of the points that Mr. Crick makes are worth considering and I am going to list just two of them. The first is that Parliament serves to inform the electorate and not to overthrow Governments. This is heresy, I suppose, for a backbench Member of the Opposition, but I am just quoting an author. He believes too much time is spent on ritualistic forms of debates and divisions on legislation which is going to be passed anyway. Here I am going to cite as an example the farm syndicate legislation which occupied us for so many days last year. The trouble is that this legislation really did not do anything. We Members should have been in the country telling the people it was not going to do anything. We have had an answer given to a written question indicating that out of the gigantic sum of $25 million the Government has allotted about a quarter of a million to this purpose. 1 know the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Mcllraith) can look at me, and I am one of the parties who took up some of the eight days on this debate. I believe we all share some of the blame.
Governments, says Mr. Crick in his second proposition, must govern. Strong Governments need strong Oppositions. Therefore the procedure of Parliament needs rethinking to fit the concept of equal access to the electorate by the parties. I do not know whether my colleagues in the other parties spend as much time as I do dropping Government news releases into that round-end filing cabinet. Some people call it "file 17", but I do not have time to call it by name. I just drop. All the engines of Government go into production to tell you the wonderful story of the record. The Opposition has rights, duties and responsibilities in the channelling of information. I believe one of the great achievements of the former Government, for example, was the establishment of the office of the Leader of the Opposition on a formal basis.
I should like to think that the Civil Service is here to serve all of us, Government or Opposition. I think they do this in most cases. However, I should like access sometimes to all the wonderful techniques of getting information to the public. Backbench Members in general should have many more facilities available to them. These facilities should include, for example, as they do in the Library of Congress at Washington, research facilities.

I think the paper prepared by Professor Denis Smith for the Special Committee on Procedure and Organization deserves most careful attention from all of us. I am grateful it has been made available to us. Mr. Speaker, the hon. Member for Royal (Mr. Fairweather), to whom I have listened attentively, said he did not wish to be drawn into the luxury of making comments on the speech which was made by my hon. friend from Timiskam-ing. I, too, hope not to be drawn into the luxury of commenting on the things which the hon. Member for Royal and others had to say. Rather, I wish to express some thoughts, some reservations, about the ideas now being proposed which have been debated for several days in this House.
In looking at the item before us I am reminded of the years I spent in the trade union movement. At the various conferences and meetings I used to attend we were invariably faced from time to time, depending on circumstances, with what we called double-barreled resolutions, that is, resolutions or motions which contained an unacceptable idea as well as an acceptable one. Without drawing an analogy here, I might add that most resolutions of this double-barreled type were introduced and fostered by adherents to the Communist party who happened to be in the trade union movement at that time. I am not implying by any means that the motion now before us had its origin in that quarter. None the less it is a double-barreled proposition containing some good points and some points which are not so good.
I am a supporter of the idea that committees should be given a larger role to play in the affairs of Parliament, that they should not become just repositories designed to alleviate some of the frustrations which backbenchers develop from time to time but rather should be an integral part of the work of our parliamentary system. This has been my contention since I came to Parliament. It has, I think, been a waste of manpower or womanpower to have established certain committees in the past. They served a relatively useless function and while they were recognized as committees in name they were for practical purposes non-existent. Therefore one of the parts of the motion before us that I appreciate and endorse is the provision that committees should play a more important role in parliamentary affairs. I do not think, though, that they will be as efficacious as some would like to believe.
I say this because there are certain built-in disadvantages which will be carried over from

DEBATES	June 3, 1965
the committee system as it now exists. One of these disadvantages is simply that the entire structure of the Civil Service in any department exists for the purpose of serving the Minister. It exists for the purpose of carrying out Government policy and for the purpose of buttressing the Minister's policy position whatever it may be. The Civil Service is not there to assist Parliament. It is not there to provide any information in real depth about a particular subject matter.
I have got to know a number of people in the public service of Canada, as have many other hon. Members. I have spoken with some of them many times on the telephone and on a number of occasions I have received comments from top ranking officials in the various Departments to the effect that they would like to give me certain information about a particular question but they were not there, as they said, to embarrass the Minister. This leaves me, as I am sure it leaves other Members who get this kind of response, in an odd position. One is left with the impression that the individual to whom one has spoken is in disagreement, probably for a technical reason, with the policy attitude taken by the Government but he is unable to express that disagreement or substantiate it with facts or statistics. Individual Members, particularly Members of the Opposition, are placed at a distinct disadvantage in their relationship to Members of the Government.
I foresee that even though a different committee structure is adopted this disadvantage which is built into the committee system at the moment will be carried over and the individual backbencher serving on any of these committees will find himself as one lone individual trying to pit his knowledge, however complete or scant it may be, against the full, massive weight and technical ability of the Civil Service of Canada which exists to serve the policy interests of the Government or of the Cabinet Minister concerned. Unless we are able and willing to provide these committees with research facilities which would place the individual Members serving on those committees on a par with the Cabinet Minister in charge of the particular Department under review, the committee system, even in its new and extended form, will over a period of time again become relatively useless so far as examination of Government policy is concerned. It will become nothing more than an educational process. Officials in the Public Service of Canada, whose purpose
June 3, 1965	COMMONS
it is to serve the policy position of Government, will be educating Members of Parliament from the point of view of the Minister on whose behalf they are speaking. The opportunity for Members serving on committees to work up detailed or substantial arguments against the policy position taken by any Government will be the same as it is now.
I see here, too, another unfortunate addition to our rules, namely, that which sets out to give greater recognition to political parties and enhance their position within Parliament. For a long time I have held the view that there has been too much political party control over parliamentary activities and not enough opportunity for the full force of the individual consciences of hon. Members to come into play. For far too long decisions have been made in the back room, as it were. Decisions have been made in caucus behind closed doors with guards outside. Even if you wanted to put an ear to the keyhole you could not get close enough to do so. For too long this has been the situation in Canada and I for one have not been in agreement with it. I have never been backward about expressing my disapproval of the degree of party control over our affairs that exists. There has not been enough freedom of expression permitted.
I submit that some of the proposed changes now before us will tend further to suppress and limit the opportunity for expression on the part of the individual Member.

I think that along with this increased authority of political parties the proposed rule unfortunately places Your Honour in a most invidious position because it gives to you the decision whether a group in this House is or is not a political party. I submit, Mr. Speaker, with all deference and without meaning this in any personal way at all, that this is none of your business. I submit it is not the business of the Speaker to determine what is a political party; I submit it is not the business of Parliament to decide what is or is not a political party. It is a decision for individuals and groups of people to make whether or not they are in or outside a party.
I submit that the proposal in suggested Standing Order 15A with respect to the Business Committee which states that "there shall be a Business Committee to which the leader of each party in the House from time to time.. . may appoint one member" leaves open to Mr. Speaker the question of determining what is or is not a party. Assume for sake of argument that the hon. Member

In answer to that question, Mr. Speaker, I just say that in my opinion any hon. Member in this House should have the right to rise to make comments about any
June 3. 1965

House of Commons Procedures subject he may wish to comment on and if he is recognized by Mr. Speaker that opportunity should be afforded him. But we are here being asked to spell out in our rules and give to Mr. Speaker the determination of what is or is not a political party. As I have said, I submit that is not the business of Mr. Speaker nor the business of this Parliament; rather it is the business of people. If in this House two hon. Members decide that they want to be a party, that should be the situation. That is their choice and decision. If a number of people who are not in this House want to form a political party as individual citizens, it is their right to go ahead and make that decision. It should not be up to other politicians to decide what is or is not a political party, for the minute we do that we politicians tend to preserve our own position.
I am sure, with all respect to the generosity of the hon. Member for York-Scarborough, that if he were given the sole determination as to what was a political party and had to enumerate two political parties, one of them would be his party. I am quite sure that any other hon. Member or politician in the same position would pick as one of the two choices the party to which he belonged. I submit this is something with which politicians should not deal and that in this sense we are making a bad move in this particular proposal.
We are also, by establishing a Business Committee and coupling with that limitations on time of debate and the like, tending to enhance and increase the authority, the position and the stature of Government, the frontbenchers, as it were, to the detriment of those who sit on the back benches. I am sure that every hon. Member when first elected to Parliament came here with a proverbial fire in his bowels and a desire to turn the world upside down if necessary in order properly to represent his constituents back home. I am also sure that many hon. Members have arrived in Parliament and have become extremely disappointed and frustrated because the opportunity to stand up and speak on behalf of their constituents was not afforded them.
During the time the Right Hon. Leader of
the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) was Prime Minister of this country and had the largest group of members of one party in our history, some 208 of them, I know that many of those members were extremely frustrated to find after coming here that they were nothing more than ciphers to vote yes or no as the Government might demand. They became fed

up and disillusioned with the whole parliamentary process because those individuals were conscientious and sincere in their desire to participate in Parliament on behalf of their constituents, but once they got here they found they were not given that recognition because of the controlling influences in Parliament resting in the hands of the frontbenchers. To this extent I think the proposed rule changes are in error.
One of the other factors which I think will work to the detriment of the private Member is the manner in which the Business Committee is likely to come to conclusions. I know the way our party operates in caucus. We have certain rules of procedure under which we meet, and I would assume that other political parties have similar rules of procedure, namely, the very normal ones that in order to come to a conclusion you must have a motion, a discussion and a vote. If on any particular issue the Conservatives meeting in caucus decided by say a 51 per cent majority, which seems to be unique for that party, that they were agreeable to a time limitation being placed on a certain item before the House and the other 49 per cent were in disagreement, I assume that majority rule would be the case and that based upon the 51 per cent decision in the Conservative caucus the Conservative Member on the Business Committee would meet with that Committee and say, "We are in favour of a time limitation". This would effectively destroy or virtually destroy the opportunity for any of the 49 per cent to express their point of view in the House about a particular item before the House for the simple reason that the decision in their caucus might result in unanimity in the Business Committee.
I would assume that the bonds are a little more rigid in the Government party, and I gather from talking to Members of that party that there is less opportunity for freedom of expression in their caucus than in the caucuses of the parties on this side. Apparently they have a stronger dictatorship in their caucus than they would like us to believe.
[DOT] (9:00 p.m.)
Any opportunity for backbenchers to participate in debate, if the situation develops as I suggest it might, will not be increased and there will not be that freedom of debate necessary to the proper functioning of the House. The one saving feature of the resolution before us is that these rules are proposed on a temporary basis, namely for the remainder of this session and the next ensuing session unless the House decides otherwise. The latter part of that suggestion I think is superfluous
June 3, 1965

because this House is the master of its own rules and it can decide otherwise at any time it so desires.
In any event, it is suggested the proposed rule changes should be adopted for a trial period so that we may see whether they work satisfactorily, at which time steps can be taken to enshrine them in our book of rules. I would venture to bet that during this and the next session the right to use the guillotine as proposed by these rule changes will not be used. I presume that the Members who negotiated these changes or designed them felt that the two sessions would take place in the same Parliament and that there might not be an intervening election. I would venture to wager also that so long as the present balance of party membership in this House is maintained the Government will not use this right of closure. The Government will want the rule changes, in effect on a temporary basis, to work smoothly with no upset so that at the end of the next ensuing session it can then suggest that they have worked well and should be made permanent.
I am not one who thinks that we should make rules which last forever. The rules of Parliament remain unchanged for too long and as a consequence the Government tends to restrict itself to a rigid application of the rules. The Government tends to become more dictatorial and take unto itself greater powers and authority. I am reminded in this regard of the powers the Government assumed during the days of the pipe line debate. That was a course which led to the downfall of the Government of that day.
I am one of those who believe that the Committee on Rules and Procedure should be a permanent standing committee and that we should regularly examine our rules and amend them. The book of rules of this House should be a living document in order that it may be used in the most effective way by Parliament itself in the interests of the Canadian people. That is what we are here to do. We are not here to enshrine our rules and we are not here to adopt changes because people say the changes are suggested by the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Mcllraith) or the Member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), those two great parliamentarians.
Our work here is to make rules which will assist us to serve the best interests of this country. I doubt very much whether the rule changes we are now considering will serve that end effectively.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when I hear appeals for precise
House of Commons Procedures speeches in the House I am reminded of what a man with religious fervour once said: "Use me, O Lord; use me-only in an advisory capacity". I think the appeals which have been made are sincere but they are indeed quite lengthy.
There is much we can do about organizing the business of this House in order to bring about a more effective result. As a junior Member I appreciate the privilege of speaking in this High Court of Parliament. I agree with the remark made last week by the hon. Member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin), that this is a supreme forum and that all Members should be heard. I know that his deputy leader in this House is of the view that Members on this side of the House should be seen, should vote but should not be heard. I am very pleased to observe support from other Members in his and other parties for the suggestion that private Members should represent their constituents, should have a voice in all issues and should be allowed to put forward ideas to the Government.
There are two issues with which I want to deal in short measure, Mr. Speaker. One relates to organizing the business of the House and the other relates to the role of the private Member.
I was very much interested in a remark made by Professor MacGregor Dawson in his book "The Government of Canada". He said:
A House of two or three hundred members which wanders where it pleases will undoubtedly be able to do a lot of wandering, but it will not accomplish much more: and if it is to perform its functions as a useful part of the government, it must be willing to place some limits on its freedom and submit to direction. It does not thereby become of necessity subservient to the Cabinet nor is the Cabinet on that account unable to derive from the House much counsel and guidance.
We have a proposal before this House to accept changes to rules and procedures on an experimental basis. I cannot see how these suggestions will abridge the rights of the Members in dealing with the business before the House.
Certainly we might look to the Mother of Parliaments, from which we have borrowed in great measure, to see how they solve this problem. The authority of Mr. Speaker is a matter of which all their Members are jealous, as we are jealous of the authority of our Speaker. It seems to me that the Speaker could well use greater authority in order to guide the deliberations of this House. In Britain the Cabinet Ministers may at the
June 3, 1965

House of Commons Procedures end of the day call for the termination of a debate, and the Speaker within his own right can accept or reject that motion and his decision cannot be appealed. If the vote is put and the business is terminated, that vote is accepted. The Members not only have the right to speak, they have the right to vote, while interminable debate denies the Members of our own House the right to come to a decision. In Britain the Government may move termination of a debate but the Speaker, in his own judgment, can accept or reject that motion. It seems to me that if we could vest that confidence in the Speaker of this House much of the discussion here could be guided in a more efficient manner.
I should like to refer to the right of a backbencher to speak. I sympathize very much with the view put forward by the hon. Member for St. Paul's (Mr. Wahn). That view was supported by the hon. Members for Broadview (Mr. Hahn), Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) and Royal (Mr. Fairweather), as well as other hon. Members of this House. Every backbencher should have the right to free expression of opinion. Of course in this House there is no list, but happy is the Member whose name appears on it. This situation reminds me of the Alice in Wonderland story about the Cheshire cat. The cat was not there, the grin certainly was. It was left behind. The historic grin of the cat is an important illustration of what goes on in many a house, possibly not this one.
[DOT] (9:10 p.m.)
It seems to me that the Whips have an important role to play. As the hon. Member for Royal (Mr. Fairweather) said, they have an important role in organizing the debate in this House. But the idea of a list submitted to the Speaker could certainly exclude Members from the debate. We should have that confidence in the Speaker to recognize those Members who rise, and let that be the determinant of whether a Member should speak. I do not think every Member should have a right to speak on every subject. If that were so, as the hon. Member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill) said last night, we would have interminable debate all the time. It is not a question whether he can speak on each subject or on each bill or on each resolution, but every hon. Member has the right to speak and to be recognized on the basis of fair selection on the part of the Speaker. If every Member's right to speak is protected even though he cannot speak every time he wishes, there is equality among the Members of the House. And the essential

issue is that the equality of Members be protected.
This is the High Court of Parliament, the supreme forum, as the hon. Member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) said. Members coming to this House come to it with a sense of responsibility not only to their constituents but to the country, conscious of the great issues confronting the world. It seems to me that the informalities, the unwritten informalities, which guide the mother of Parliaments certainly have had a great influence on this Parliament and could do much to guide us in making our deliberations orderly, informed and effective.
I should like to read a few lines from A. V. Dicey, the great British scholar, in his book "The Law of the Constitution". At page 469 he says this:
The constitution when thus looked at ceases to appear a "sort of maze": it is seen to consist of two different parts; the one part is made up of understandings, customs, or conventions which, not being enforced by the courts, are in no true sense of the word laws; the other part is made up of rules which are enforced by the courts, and which, whether embodied in statutes or not, are laws in the strictest sense of the term, and make up the true law of the constitution.
It has been the glory of the British constitution and the workings of parliamentary democracy in Britain that that unwritten law underlying our great tradition of parliamentary democracy has ensured the growth and the strength of parliamentary institutions. It seems to me that in this House we can gain strength from ensuring that the parliamentary tradition which we have built up and which we are reinforcing with these measures through written as well as unwritten constitutions can strengthen Parliament. I believe, Mr. Speaker, that the role of the Speaker is something which can be much more effective and important if we, the Members of this House, have that sense of confidence in the judgment of a Speaker whom we choose. I believe the unwritten constitution of which Dicey spoke is a sure guardian of our rights in this House.

tory view before the public and before this House.
The hon. Member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) made a very eloquent appeal this afternoon for the rights of the private Member and stated unequivocally his position, which was that he was against a time limit on a debate because this would put too much power in the hands of the party Whips, would limit the role of the private Member, and therefore in some way we would lose a great deal of our rights. Yet, Mr. Speaker, this is the party which sort of jumped the gun on the Committee on Procedure and Organization which we set up last session. It is the party which, with great fanfare, produced a press release to the nation calling for allocation of time for debate.
I should like to quote one paragraph from this press release or communique which I have in my hand, issued under the name of the leader of that parliamentary group, just to indicate what was proposed at that time. The date of the communique is September 22, 1964, and I quote from paragraph 4 on page 2:
That an allocation of time order be adopted, under which, by all-party agreement before any stage of debate commences, the length of time for any such stage of debate could be determined by the house, just as certain debates already have a time limit fixed in advance by a rule of the house.
To me, after listening to the hon. Member for Timiskaming, the hon. Member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Barnett) and the hon. Member for Skeena (Mr. Howard) this evening, their remarks indicate once more the hypocrisy of the situation. Reform appeared to be a popular measure last fall and certainly was something which could be used by that group to attract some attention. They were for reform. They were going to reform this institution. But when they are called upon to put up we find them singing a different tune.
This evening the hon. Member for Skeena argued that we should not have any identification of a party system, that we should not have a party control in the House, and that these new rules were in some way going to give parties in this House some special status. Yet this is the group, Mr. Speaker, which a couple of weeks ago in the budget debate were insisting on their rights and were attempting to deny the opportunity to a backbench Member on this side of the House to speak in this debate. I happened to be at that time the victim of these tactics so therefore I feel somewhat strongly about this.
House of Commons Procedures
According to the members of that group, opportunities for backbenchers to speak should be afforded to the members of that group. Then they are perfectly willing to bring forward, propaganda, election material, as did the hon. Member for Hamilton, which indicates who are the Members working for the people. Having demanded and weasled various opportunities for debate in this House, they use those opportunities for propaganda purposes in their ridings. They are the Members who do more talking in this chamber than Members on this side of the House.
We have been criticized, Mr. Speaker, for being a House of too much discussion. This group is supposed to be the party of reform. Yet I would wager on any analysis of the speaking time taken up in this House by Members that a disproportionate time has been allocated to Members of that group. To me, Mr. Speaker, this is absolute hypocrisy in view of the position demonstrated by the New Democratic Party.
The hon. Member for Skeena indicated this evening that it was only by custom that on motions the Speaker recognized the representatives of the various groups. He was not, of course, accurate in that statement.

A spokesman for each of the parties in opposition to the Government may comment briefly, subject to the same limitation.

Member for Skeena, statements on motions. We only have to be here a very short time, and I am a new Member, Mr. Speaker, to realize it would be

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this House generally is composed of a group of amateurs and I am one of them. I have heard a great deal during this debate about the right to speak. I want to say at the start that the gist of my speech tonight will be on the subject of the right to speak. Apparently we must go back to our A, B, C's to ascertain why we are here. We are here now to speak and I for one think we are here under false pretences if we do not speak when we are here. It is not necessary to be an expert in every field in order to speak. I for one represent what we used to call the little people of Canada, the people who pay the bills. When the Government makes its proposals it is my job as a representative of the little people, the taxpayers, to be convinced that the spending of this money or the implementation of these policies is something which is not going to harm unduly either the pocketbooks of those taxpayers or their liberties.
We live in a democracy, at least we still call it one, although from time to time I see that the walls of closure and the walls of silence are creeping upon us. We are not even allowed to speak, in the opinion of some people. We are to take the opinions of the establishment, that silent group that sits behind the press, behind Parliament, behind the campaign funds and behind certain lobbies outside. They will make the decisions and we are to sit here in silence and suffer them. Then we have the Civil Service, an ever increasing body of important, well-informed people and specialists. They sit in their own little ivory towers making policies which are presented through certain assorted Cabinet Ministers. We are supposed to swallow them hook, line and sinker. In the view of the people of my constituency I am not paid to come here and quietly accept these iced cakes which, in my opinion, are often full of sawdust.
We choose certain assorted Cabinet Ministers, usually with regard to the territory from which they come and not their ability. They sit in conclaves and make official decisions as to what they shall present to us in the House. Once again, we are expected to sit here and clap like trained seals as a well organized political party might do. This party for one is not that type of organized political party. We have retained our amateur stand-

ing. We are going to sit here, whether or not we are uninformed, and ride herd on those groups to whom I have just referred. All the dangerous groups are not in Parliament. They do not all sit on my left. I have just enumerated some of them. Sometimes the establishment can be a dangerous group; sometimes the Civil Service can be a dangerous group; sometimes the Government and Cabinet can be a very dangerous group. It is our job to sit here, with our meagre amateur ability and our amateur opinions, in the only free forum in Canada which is paid for by the people we represent and say what we want. In some cases it is the only method by which the little people have a chance to be heard. I am against any rules which unnecessarily curb our right to speak.
The parliamentary system is not perfect but it is the best system we have yet achieved to protect the rights of the little people against those groups, in or out of Parliament, who sometimes do not know how to give these people the rights, liberties and freedom which they so greatly need and deserve today. I do not believe we have been doing as good as job as we should have been doing in this regard. This is why I do not walk out behind the curtain and say it is a hopeless mess. I do not believe it is a hopeless mess but it will be if we have rules which tie our freedom so tightly we are not allowed to stand up here and say what we think.
In my opinion one of the weaknesses of the parliamentary system is that we run it like a lawsuit. It is necessary to have a prosecution and a defence. We have, therefore, evolved the party system under which you can be for or against something. I do not believe we can complain that there is not enough party discipline when 127 out of a party of 128 can vote for something like the flag without a murmur. Trained seals they might be, when only one dissents, but I think you have plenty of party discipline. It is because the Government of the day can line these people up and make them vote the same way that the Opposition should be strong. We will not be able to stand up against these dangerous groups in this Parliament if we do not have some way of standing as a group and saying yes or no. I do not know how you can perform in a court of law if you have four or five different lawyers prosecuting a case from four or five different points of view or, in other words, trying to prove whether or not this Government is fit to run this country for five years.
June 3, 1965	COMMONS
I do not want to digress and say when I think we lost one of the most important rules which decides whether or not a Government can be disciplined by an Opposition. However,
I want to touch on it very briefly. Back in 1925, when Mr. Meighen and the then Prime Minister of Canada, Mr. King, were fighting their lawsuit and prosecuting one another, the people of Canada were bamboozled into a position where they thought the issue was one as to whether or not they were going to be governed from Westminster or in Canada. The election was won on that basis and the Liberals were swept back into power. Mr. Meighen suffered a defeat and the liberties of the people of Canada suffered a defeat from which we have not yet recovered. The reason I say so is that from that day forward the Prime Minister of Canada has had the right to dissolve Parliament and there is no higher authority in existence to prevent him from forcing an election upon the electorate of Canada ten days after they have expressed their will in a previous election.
[DOT] (9:30 p.m.)
This gives him a power over the people of Canada which he was never intended to have under our parliamentary system and this is probably at the root of many of the difficulties we have today. A minority Government can be in a position to run this country with about 27 per cent or 28 per cent of the electorate behind it merely because the Prime Minister can say at any time, "You face an election." When that happens Parliament is dissolved and the people of Canada are subjected to extreme expense.
We should go back to the position in 1925 with the Governor General having the power to summon an alternative to the Government any time the Government does not have majority support in the House of Commons.
I venture to say that if the present Members of the House were to stand and vote according to their conscience this Government would not have 51 per cent of the vote in the House.
I am tired of hearing from the so-called groups, smaller political parties, or whatever you want to call them, continual criticism of the Government because when it comes to making a decision on whether the Government is fit to be in office they always support it, even though they say they are fed up and disgusted with it. We are also fed up and disgusted with many of the things the Government has done, and I may say that any time I have stood up and voted I have voted to get it out of office as soon as possible.
DEBATES	1965
House of Commons Procedures If we want to get away from hypocrisy and make Parliament run smoothly, we need to do nothing more than stand up and be counted. I say to those people in the smaller groups, if you have confidence in the Government then join it lock, stock and barrel. Make your deals with the Government. Get into the Cabinet. Let the people of Canada know you have confidence in the Government.
We are not going to get better Government by restricting the voting or talking power of anybody in the House. I am against putting rules into the book which will restrict us, but this does not mean to say I think every Member should get up and talk about every subject. Indeed, quite the contrary. I am as tired as you are, Mr. Speaker, of hearing people talk on subjects about which they know nothing. You may have been bored many times when I have done so. Nevertheless, when it comes to the price of pigs, selling wheat to China or doing something about the unemployment situation, every man who has earned his living by the sweat of his brow knows about these subjects, although these very subjects are seldom discussed in the House.
We talked about the flag for four or five months and this party was criticized for doing so. One of the reasons we did so was that there was nothing else solid to talk about. The Government in office can decide those subjects on which we are going to talk.
Each session we start with the Speech from the Throne which should and sometimes does give us the agenda which we will discuss for the ensuing year. But the last Speech from the Throne was so general that we could get up and talk about anything. The rule book cannot restrict us if we want to talk about everything in the Speech from the Throne because it covered the waterfront without saying anything.
If the Speech from the Throne is not an agenda for us, then one of the rules we might adopt in written form or by practice is one by which we will know what we are going to talk about while we are here. I do not think we should be here 12 months a year but if we are we should at least know what we are going to talk about.
The press always criticizes us for not being here. I am quite sure the attendance would be much better if we knew what we were going to talk about when we are here. I do not know why we should be here 12 months a year unless we are representing the people of the country, but how can we do that unless
June 3, 1965

House of Commons Procedures we get back to the country and talk to the people there who are paying the bills?
On occasion we are also criticized for talking too much. One of these days I want an opportunity to talk about agriculture in the House. We have talked very little about it and it is one of the questions bothering the country. The people of my district are not the slightest bit interested in rules of procedure. I do not expect they will read this debate and I will not even bother to send them copies of it.
I am talking to the Members here. Perhaps it is like the parson talking to the empty pews in church. Both front benches are comparatively empty, numerically empty, and it is they who set the policy or are supposed to do to. They are the ones who want reform but apparently they do not want to hear backbenchers speaking about reforms. We would be delighted to sit here and listen to their solid suggestions to make this Parliament better, but if such suggestions do not come from the front benches then the front benches should be changed.
I for one came down here expecting to listen for ten years. I have only been here seven.

speechtext:
I did not come down here to be a school teacher or a trainer of Cabinet Ministers. I came here to learn and I have kept my ears open. Somebody might say they are big enough. They are big enough to hear and I am quite willing to learn. But I want a little more leadership and I want to know what is going wrong because I, like the rest of the people of Canada, am seriously worried about the things which are left undone.
Sometimes I am worried about those things which are done and if some of them continue to be done the Government will hear a great deal more criticism. If it does not show a little more leadership it will get more criticism. The people of Canada are waking up and they will not be put oil by arguments about procedure. They want solid suggestions for improvement. They do not want pious talk about a war on poverty. They want to see poverty disappear.
We are tired of hearing about equal rights in Alabama. I want to know when the Indians in my district are going to have their commission set up so they can get equal rights in Canada. I have no time to go marching in Alabama. But apparently I am not allowed to march back to Athabasca once in a

while to get in touch with people there who are suffering badly. There are still people in this country who are sleeping on piles of rags on wooden floors, sometimes not even wooden floors but snowbanks and mud. Some of them are sleeping on the front benches.
[DOT] (9:40 p.m.)
In case somebody thinks I may be wandering a little I want to say I do not see any reason why our rules should be drastically changed. It is the general principles on which we are falling down. It is not a question of failing to recognize the rights of the smaller parties in this House. I think it is a matter of record that when we had 208 Members we refused to use our preponderance of numbers to bully the smaller parties; we leaned over backwards to give them the chance to speak. We gave them more opportunity to speak than they perhaps should have had. They spoke at great length. I remember one filibuster during which they withheld consent to legislation dissolving marriage for a period up to two years. In the end they made their point and I do not see how they can argue now that unlimited debate is always wrong.
I do not see how debate can be limited except by decency and common sense. We choose a Speaker from our midst. We have had good Speakers during all of the time I have been in this House. They have exercised great restraint, great common sense, great patience and, by and large, tremendous fairness. If there has been any fault it has been expressed by leaning over backward in favour of the smaller groups. Even those who may be taking far too long are given full right to speak. I go further. I think we should waste a thousand hours in this House rather than deny any well-intentioned Member his right to speak, amateur though he may be, long-winded though he may be. He may have to speak for two years before gaining his point. I have not yet passed judgment on what happened with regard to those divorce cases. If the action taken at that time was well-intentioned and if the result was a proper one, I think it was not only a privilege but a right and a duty for Members to speak until their consciences were clear and they had done what they had undertaken to do for those people who put them here, the only forum in which their will could be expressed.
I believe common sense is not entirely dead in Canada and while we have Speakers of the quality we have had during the last seven years I believe our rights and privileges are in good hands. Do the people of Canada really believe we are wasting all our time and not
June 3, 1965	COMMONS
earning our keep? If they do, they can replace this House from top to bottom, all 265 members. They still have that privilege. I do not think juggling the rules can make any difference. If we take a good look at ourselves and the job we came here to do and act according to our consciences we can still discipline any Government which takes over. We still have the right to act according to our consciences. If we choose not to do so, we have no one to blame but ourselves; we cannot point to a little green book and say: "Rule 29 or rule 36 prevents me from being a Canadian. We are speaking our minds in the most powerful court in the land. We can do anything legally in this court. We can change our constitution-

We can change our form of Government. We can make and break Cabinet Ministers. We can throw Governments out of office. It is not good enough to sit back and say: I do not like the way the Prime Minister does this or that. Some hon. Members are always talking about the way they do things in England. Well, Pym and Hampden, Pitt and Fox and Burke would not have sat around blaming the rule book. They would not have blamed the Queen or her ancestors. When one of Britain's Kings did not do what he should have done-they only did this to one of them -they took him out on the front porch and gave him a very close haircut. We could do it yet. We do not need to do it. But the example is in history. Prime Ministers and Governments have been defeated before now. I am not talking particularly about this administration. I am talking about the opposition as a whole. If the united opposition in Canada wants to give Canada good, clean government then the first thing to do is to get rid of those fellows over there, then stop whining and get down to business and do our job in this House. And our job in this House is to stop bickering.
I do not know how long it takes to make a point. A man should be able to make his point in two minutes. I am allowed 40 minutes. It is not the length of one's speech that counts. It is not even what is said. It is a combination of what you say and who is listening, and, having listened, what they are going to do about it.

Somebody said tonight that Parliament is the art of compromise. I will tell the House what I think about that. I think
DEBATES	1967
House of Commons Procedures the art of compromise should only be brought into play after you have fought for what you believe in with every ounce of energy and every grain of intelligence you possess. Let us not compromise to the point at which we become so openminded that our brains fall out. If there is something you believe in, do not only stand up and say so but stick to your guns while you are sitting in your seat as well as when you are standing on your feet. Politics is war. It is a war without guns, I suppose, but it requires as much guts, integrity and patriotism as any war you will ever get into. I ought to know because I have been in the shooting line and this is tougher.
We are mixed up in a war where I cannot wait for the corporal to come and tell me what to do. I happen to be on the spot. You can say we are all privates or perhaps that we are all generals. But I am responsible for what I do. I am getting tired of blaming the little green book or of blaming the Prime Minister for not doing his job. I am not sure whether he is doing it. He may be doing it to the best of his ability. We talk about cooperation and togetherness. We hear it said: Let all the parties get together and agree on the things which have to be done. As I read my history book, and I have read it, the greatest improvements in democratic affairs have always been brought about when there has been a clearcut division along party lines, when Conservatives knew what Conservatives were and when Liberals knew what real Liberalism meant. Real Liberalism in Gladstone's day worked against vested interests and tried to get a better deal for the little man. Where has that kind of Liberalism gone?

I am not altogether satisfied with Conservatism either. Sometimes I think we get on the socialist bandwagon and try to outdo the socialists. It cannot be done. The confusion which pervades the socialist ranks is something we can never match. So let us get on with private enterprise, give those who want to fight for it leadership in the private enterprise field and ensure that they have a strong and vigorous party behind which to rally every day. It is not that I do not believe in looking after the old people. After all, the old people are looked after whether they live in a Communist country or whether they live among the Incas of Peru. Surely we in Canada will always be able to do at least as well.
June 3, 1965

House of Commons Procedures [DOT] (9:50 p.m.)
There should be two well defined parties in the House, those who think the Government is doing well and those who think it is not. I should like to see anybody who thinks it is not doing well come over to the side of the House where they can vote "nay". I assure you, gentlemen, that if you gave me the kind of leadership that you think you are giving I would not hesitate to cross the floor of the House. But you are so wrong. I would be willing to support the Prime Minister in any policies up until the statutory time of calling another election as long as he gave me the kind of world leadership that he had by reputation before he took the reins of Government. He has ability and I would like to see some of that ability channelled into forthright leadership, honest government and clearcut policies. I say: "Don't try to ride the Socialist wagon. If you are Liberals, go the Liberal way". Is is clear enough; read the history books and see what Gladstone, Laurier and other famous Liberals did. Follow that policy and victory will be in your hands but if you follow the pink policy I think the Canadian people will reject you.
The reforms we need are reforms of character and leadership in government, not reforms in the rules. I do not think we have to recognize more than two parties in this House, and I believe that any contrary rule put into the rule book would weaken the two party system and would be a retrograde step. I think the two party system is always good, not for reds and blues, not necessarily for ins and outs, but for those who support the avowed policies outlined in the Speech from the Throne, if you can find clearcut policies in the Speech from the Throne. If you cannot, we should meet immediately after the Speech from the Throne has been read and vote that government out so we can get a group together which can lay down a policy which we can understand and on which we can vote yea or nay upon the first day this House sits.

We can amend the Constitution, which after all is just our big rule book. Let us put into the Constitution the power of an independent arbitrator or a referee of some sort, whether it be the Queen, the Governor General or whether he is called something else. maintopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS-SAINT JOHN, N.B.- REPORTED DEPOSIT REQUIREMENT TO OBTAIN EMPLOYMENT
LABOUR CONDITIONS-SAINT JOHN, N.B.- REPORTED DEPOSIT REQUIREMENT TO OBTAIN EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the other day, as shown at page 1767 of Hansard, I posed a question to the Minister of Labour (Mr. MacEachen) regarding employment practices for the M/V Boylen. The Minister's response was that there was some difficulty in determining just which company did the hiring and, second:
[DOT] (10:00 p.m.)
Apparently the payment of $400 by members of the crew Is limited to German personnel who have been flown over to Canada. These crew members were, I understand, required to sign a service contract designed to guarantee a refund of air transportation costs.
I consider this to be a requirement that individual crew members purchase their jobs, a practice which disappeared in Canada many years ago.
In respect of this situation, I should like to refer to a copy of one of the service contracts and read extracts from it. I will make this copy, as well as my entire file, available to the Minister in the event he does not already have this information. This service contract is in respect of one Johann Wenke and states that Kent Line Ltd., as agents for Engineering Consultants Ltd., Saint John, N.B., and the Irving Oil Company, Saint John, N.B., is the employer. That statement will perhaps eliminate any difficulty in deciding who employs these people.
June 3, 1965

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
The Minister stated that he understood the $400 was a guarantee that the air transportation costs would not be lost if an employee left the ship before completing the contract, in the event that employee had been flown to Canada. Let me read part of this contract which was signed, incidentally, in Hamburg on March 25, 1965. It states:
The employee deposits with the company the amount of Can-$400-as security for completion of this contract. The company binds itself by obligation to return this sum to the employee on the date of expiration of this contract.
There is no reference there to air transportation costs and no reference to the fact that these individuals have been flown over to Canada. I repeat that this contract was signed in Hamburg on March 25 of this year. Incidentally, almost the entire crew of the M/V Boylen are German, so that when the Minister suggests that this applies only to German personnel this means in effect that it applies to the entire crew. This contract sets out the wage scale as being $150 per month, minimum, to $210, maximum, Canadian funds. Surely in view of those salaries a deposit of $400 on the part of an employee is a bit of an imposition and an exploitation of the individual.
There is another interesting feature of this service contract which I submit interferes with the basic rights of an individual to proceed through the courts of this land. Clause 13 of the contract states:
The rights and obligations of the parties are to be governed by the Laws of the Province of New Brunswick, Canada. All disputes arising between the Master or Company and the Employee regarding this agreement shall be heard only in the courts of the Province of New Brunswick, Canada.
I am sure if the Minister looks into that situation he will find that that is an infringement upon the rights of individuals to proceed through the courts, even to the Supreme Court of Canada in the event the individual considers he has received improper or unfair treatment from a lower court.
Returning to the contract itself and the requirement that $400 be deposited, I suggest that this is in effect job buying. The Irving Oil Company, a virtual dictator in the province of New Brunswick, acting as the employer, is interfering with the rights and freedoms of the individuals involved in this situation. I submit it is the Government's responsibility, particularly inasmuch as this is a matter concerning shipping and comes under the jurisdiction of the Federal Government, to act to protect the rights of these individuals.
As I said, Mr. Speaker, I will be glad to make available to the Minister all the documents I have here, some of which refer to the safety measures aboard ship and other such subjects, but I have confined my remarks tonight purely to the employee-employer relationship that exists and I ask the Minister seriously to look into this matter and take the necessary corrective measures.

speakeroldname: Hon. A. J. MacEachen (Minister of Labour):
maintopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS-SAINT JOHN, N.B.- REPORTED DEPOSIT REQUIREMENT TO OBTAIN EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have, following the question raised originally by the hon. Member for Timiskaming, asked the chief officer of the Canada Labour Relations Board in Fredericton, New Brunswick, to check into this matter, and as a result he directed an inquiry to the firm of McKelvey, Macaulay, Machum and Fairweather, who replied in connection with the M/V Boylen. The information contained in this letter is as follows:
In reply to your enquiry I am enclosing a copy of an addendum to the service contract signed by Germans hired for the crew of the above vessel setting out the details of the advance of $400 made to such crew members and the security deposit of $400 to guarantee performance of their service contracts. The advance is repaid by monthly holdbacks of $40 and the $400 is paid over to the man on due fulfilment of his service contract.
The service contract requires crew members to serve for at least 12 months. The present system became necessary when many German crew members deserted without completing their service contracts and without repaying the monies advanced for travel and hiring costs; they were thus using employment on this vessel as a means of immigrating to Canada at someone else's expense. The advance-deposit-holdback system was inaugurated to counteract this practice and has proven to be satisfactory.
These crew members do not in any way "buy their jobs" as suggested by the question raised in the House of Commons.
That is the explanation we have received. In the light of the comments made by the hon. Member I will be glad to examine the situation, consider his comments and, if necessary, request further information.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on May 28 during the question

June 3, 1965
period I addressed the following question to the Minister of Labour, as reported at page 1769 of Hansard:
I am informed that some time ago one Harold Chamberlain Banks, one Leonard McLaughlin and one Norman Cunningham were charged with conspiring to commit an assault against one Richard Greaves in Vancouver. I am also informed that the charge against Mr. Banks has been dropped because he is on vacation in the United States...
I would like to ask the Minister whether he has any knowledge as to why the charges against Leonard McLaughlin and Norman Cunningham have not been proceeded with.
I addressed the question to the Minister of Labour because I thought it was a labour matter and he would be directly concerned with it. Possibly I should have directed it to the Minister of Justice and I must apologize for disturbing his program for this evening.
[DOT] (10:10 p.m.)
I was asked to ask this question by a number of persons who are very interested in preserving the good name of the labour movement in Canada, including some people who are quite important in C.L.C. unions in this country. I was informed that the Crown in the name of Canada did intend to lay charges but Mr. Harold Chamberlain Banks had left the country and they were dropped. I understand consideration is being given to laying charges against Harold Chamberlain Banks, Leonard McLaughlin and Norman Cunningham for conspiracy to commit an assault against Richard Greaves in Vancouver on June 30, 1960.
I was informed also that Richard Greaves was visited by members of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and told to be prepared to appear as a witness in a court case in this connection in Montreal in August, 1964. He was informed also that prosecuting attorney for the Royal Canadian Mounted Police would be one J. Martineau. I was later informed, Mr. Speaker, that a man named Clayton Statton did beat one Richard Greaves at the time I mentioned. This man Statton was imported from the United States by one Rod Heinekey, a gentleman who was recently elected as executive vice-president of the Seafarers' International Union of Canada. I understand that Mr. Heinekey had to put up a $500 bond because this man Statton had committed a previous assault in Canada. Mr. Heinekey at the time claimed that he was a personal friend of his. I am informed also that later this Clayton Statton attacked a recluse in Vancouver who thought he was going to be robbed. During the struggle Clayton Statton was killed by the accidental dis-22620-126
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion charge of his own gun which he apparently carried with him.
I raise this question, Mr. Speaker, at the request of those persons I mentioned who are interested in preserving the good name of the labour movement in Canada. X think that in fairness both to the person who was attacked and the accused these cases should be prosecuted and should not be dropped. It is my opinion such action should be taken to clear up the situation. I should like very much to have the Minister of Justice (Mr. Favreau) inform the House why these cases were not proceeded with.

speechtext:
No, because I do not want to give mine away either.
For the information of the hon. Member I must say that the charge against Banks has not been dropped. Banks has been charged with conspiracy to assault one Greaves, and in the charge one Cunningham and one McLaughlin have been named, on the advice of counsel, as co-conspirators. They have not been charged. I am advised that this is a practice in many cases where counsel is of the opinion there is not sufficient evidence to prove completely a charge of conspiracy, to name one or more persons as co-conspirators, thus allowing the complete charge to be proven more fully against one such as Banks against whom it is felt there is sufficient evidence.
However, Banks went through his preliminary inquiry and was committed for trial. In circumstances of which we are all aware he failed to present himself for his trial. This is what my hon. friend refers to as the holiday which Banks is presently taking. Therefore proceedings are still pending against him. I am quite sure that the bail was forfeited although for purposes of this discussion I did not bring my attention to bear specifically on that matter.
I hope these intimations are sufficient for the moment, and I should be pleased to discuss the matter further and pertinently with the hon. Member should he feel he needs additional information.

maintopic: ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE-VANCOUVER- DISPOSITION OF ASSAULT CHARGES AGAINST S.I.U. MEMBERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I raise a question regarding a series of articles appearing in the Toronto Telegram, the fourth of which appears in today's issue, concerning the R.C.M.P. and written by Robert Macdonald.
The first article started off this way:
R.C.M.P. Commissioner George W. McClellan, harassed from all sides in recent months, has spoken out against detractors of the force.
"There are certain elements in this country who would destroy this force," the Commissioner said.
Speaking with a forthrightness never before displayed by an R.C.M.P. Commissioner, he told this writer-
Then the article goes on to deal with an R.C.M.P. overhaul. Later the writer says:
He-
Commissioner McClellan.
-appears tired of the public criticism heaped on his 7,000-man police force, and weary of waiting for a government champion to defend the force in the House of Commons.
The Commissioner sees sinister agencies at work undermining the efficiency of the force.
"This is part of their over-all plan to destroy, subvert and create mistrust in the free world," he said.
Parliamentary criticism has certainly had an effect on morale-it has a disturbing effect on the man whose heart is in this force, he said.
What caused the Commissioner to open up so forcefully?
The frustrations stemming from the four-month Dorion inquiry during which the R.C.M.P. was attacked day after day was one reason. But it was also due to the recurrent attacks on the force that have been launched in recent years by politicians.
In the first article which appeared on May 29 the writer said:
The real breakdown in government liaison with the R.C.M.P. came during the period Lionel Chevrier was Justice Minister, according to one top officer.
"The man didn't even know where our office was," he said.
So it goes, with a larding of quotations from Commissioner McClellan. Not too long ago Commissioner McClellan wrote a letter to the C.B.C. regarding a "Viewpoint" program in which Anthony Wright, a Canadian who comes from Britain, who served in the British armed forces and happens to be the representative in the Press Gallery for the West German Press Service, made a critique of the R.C.M.P.
When you get a Commissioner who writes a letter and then reveals it in public and names four times this representative of the West German Press Service, then you have a man who has a bit of bigotry and bias in his
[Mr. Favreau.l

soul. He is trying to appeal from the basis of anti-German sentiment. Beyond that, what he has done in his letter to the C.B.C. is to miss the whole point about free comment in this country on a program like "Viewpoint". Even the fact that he sent it to the news department of the C.B.C. instead of recognizing the public affairs role of the C.B.C. is an indication that he is the kind of man I for one should begin to have some doubts about.
When he talks about sinister forces at work trying to destroy the R.C.M.P., and the inference is directed at Parliament, then we have a pretty serious situation on hand if this is the true picture and if Commissioner McClellan is properly quoted in his remarks about the West German Press Representative and his comment about sinister forces. If we have reached the stage where we cannot be critical of the R.C.M.P., its education and its training, if we have reached the stage where we cannot make suggestions in regard to isolating the security and intelligence directorate from the rest of the R.C.M.P. without incurring these suggestions that such criticisms are part of a sinister force, then I do not know where parliamentarians are going to be. I should like to point out to the Minister that the only occasion, apart from the Doukhobor disturbances, when this country has faced violence has been in connection with the separatist movement in Quebec. Where was the R.C.M.P.? We had a story here the other day, "Tailed into Toilet by The R.C.M.P.". But when we did have the one recent threat to our security, where was the R.C.M.P.?
[DOT] (10:20 p.m.)
I should like to make one final point in bringing this allegation about "sinister forces" to the attention of the Minister. The Canadian Association of University Teachers in 1963, 1964 was and, to my knowledge, in 1965 is still critical of R.C.M.P. tactics on the campus. I am critical of R.C.M.P. tactics in the whole field of investigating citizenship and security risks among ordinary citizens. If by being critical we represent sinister forces, then I think the R.C.M.P. or its commissioner should be the subject of attention by some kind of commission or inquiry. That is why I raised this question with the Minister in the House, a question to which I think we deserve an answer. I know he cannot give a proper answer in three minutes but I take a serious view of the picture which is beginning to form in my mind and in the minds of other people about this gentleman who is the head of the R.C.M.P. and the views he has on democracy under our parliamentary system.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE-VANCOUVER- DISPOSITION OF ASSAULT CHARGES AGAINST S.I.U. MEMBERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thought the question was to be limited to the article as such and whatever comments 1 had to make on it. For this reason, as the hon. Member himself noted, I am unable in the time at my disposal to answer all the points he has raised.
I discussed with Commissioner McClellan of the R.C.M.P. the article appearing in the Toronto Telegram of May 29. I am satisfied that the information which he gave to the reporter was given in the best interest of the R.C.M.P. and of the Canadian public and was appropriate and accurate. Without taking personal issue with any of the critics referred to by the reporter and who included the hon. Member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher), he showed how and why their criticism was ill-founded and unfair.
Concerning the elements in this country who would destroy the forces as part of their over-all plan to destroy, subvert, and create mistrust in the free world, Commissioner McClellan advised me that he had made reference to those criminal and subversive elements which are constantly at work in our country, as well as others, to impede and render ineffective the efforts not only of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police but all police forces in Canada to protect the security and peace of the nation. He has assured me, though I might say I needed no such assurance from him in this respect, that he said nothing intended to reflect in the slightest degree any criticism of the Government or its Ministers. He did not make any personal reference to my predecessor, Mr. Chevrier.
DEBATES	1973
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
I fully share Commissioner McClellan's great pride in the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and its achievements, a Force which he has served for 33 years. I might remind those who criticize the training and education of members of the Force that senior police officers from all over the world seek an opportunity for specialized and advanced training in the Royal Canadian Mounted Police schools and laboratories. Furthermore, requests are being received from countries throughout the world for the assistance of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police in organizing or modernizing police forces. It is perhaps significant in view of what I have just said that the first successful use of mass communication by satellite for the apprehension of a wanted man was made by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police.
I share with the Commissioner his concern, in the face of frequent unfounded criticism, for the morale of his men who have no voice of their own and who have as the Toronto Telegram put it, a stupendous task in a huge country. I also understand his problem in recruiting suitable candidates for a police career in the face of such criticism.
As Minister of Justice I fully comprehend the need for public vigilance in matters of law enforcement, but it adds nothing to constructive criticism when public servants who have devoted their lives to the protection of the public are referred to even by certain Members of this House in the contemptuous manner quoted in the Toronto Telegram.
